summary_md: Sessions 1 and 2 set the frame for the whole course. Software engineering is a systematic process, not just writing code, and this is "not a Python course": it is about what happens to a program once teammates are involved. You learn the ways working code still fails and the practice that answers each, the seven phases of the software development lifecycle on the expense tracker, and why software is maintained far longer than it is written. Session 2 then compares Waterfall and Agile: where each genuinely works, how to read the Agile Manifesto correctly, what Scrum, Kanban, XP and Lean prescribe, and which parts this course borrows.
exam_focus_md:
- A short team story: name the failure from session 1's slide 6 and the answer from its slide 8 (Agile and Scrum; clean code, testing, TDD; version control, review, CI; containers and automatic deployment).
- Four changes to a program: which one is the refactoring, the bug fix, the feature or the tech debt (the shape of sample Q2).
- A decision or artefact (a feature table, a sketch of the structure, a checklist): which SDLC phase it belongs to, and which decisions reach more than one phase.
- A project scenario (a regulated fixed-price contract, a start-up, a support desk): which approach fits and why, argued from session 2's slides 6, 7 and 13.
- A teammate's reading of the Agile Manifesto ("so we skip the README"): what the values actually rank.
- Open, 5–8 lines: compare Waterfall and Agile for a given project, including a usable first iteration and one real downside of Agile.
- Combined with later sessions: a pytest or uv transcript in which you name the session 1 failure it shows.

sections.heading: Software engineering, and the ways working code still fails
sections.body_md:
Software engineering, in the course's definition, is "the systematic process of designing, developing, testing, and maintaining computer software using scientific and engineering principles". It goes beyond writing code: it is the structured approach that keeps a program **reliable, secure, efficient, and easy to maintain over time**.

That is why session 1 says this is **not a Python course**. Syntax is assumed (loops, functions, types, one completed Python course), and new constructs arrive "as design tools, not language tourism". The goal is what happens to the little program you wrote **once three teammates get involved** and it has to run reliably, be easy to change, and be trustworthy.

Slide 6 lists the ways working code still fails once other people and time are involved (its title says six; it lists the five below). Slide 8 puts a methodology or a tool against each:

| What goes wrong | What it looks like | The course's answer |
|---|---|---|
| "Works on my machine", and nowhere else | It runs for its author; on a teammate's laptop or a server it does not | Containerisation, automatic deployment |
| A teammate's code change breaks the build | One person's change lands and the shared project stops passing its checks | Version control, code reviews, CI |
| Six months on, nobody can read it, not even its author | Names like `d`, `r`, `x`; the comment on slide 7 admitting that only god now knows how the routine works | Clean code, testing, TDD |
| Change one thing, three others break, silently | A small edit quietly breaks behaviour somewhere else and nothing tells you | Clean code, testing, TDD |
| No shared plan, four people build four corners | Each member builds the part they imagined; the parts never add up to one product | Agile, Scrum |

Slide 8 groups the two middle failures as "unreadable, breaks silently". The tools are "a curated, opinionated selection": pytest, git, GitHub, Docker. Session 3 adds that "works on my machine" is "the single problem this whole course is built to solve", which is why uv installs the same versions for everyone from the very first lab.

Read the table as the map of the term: every later session is one of these answers. When an exam story describes a team in trouble, first name the failure, then the practice that prevents it.
key_points: Software engineering is a systematic process (design, develop, test, maintain) that keeps software reliable, secure, efficient and easy to maintain.
Not a Python course: it is about what happens to code once teammates are involved.

No shared plan → Agile, Scrum. Unreadable, breaks silently → clean code, testing, TDD. Change breaks the build → version control, code reviews, CI. Works on my machine → containerisation, automatic deployment.
Name the failure first, then the practice that answers it.
sections.exam_note_md: Expect a short team story: you name the failure from slide 6 and the answer from slide 8. Keep the pairings exact; vague answers such as "better teamwork" score nothing.

sections.heading: The SDLC: seven phases on the expense tracker
sections.body_md:
The **software development lifecycle (SDLC)** is the sequence of phases software goes through: **Idea, Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance**. Following it, "we build and protect the software *before* users get to it". One sentence sets up session 2: "The methodology lies in how we transition from one phase to the next."

Session 1 walks through the phases with one example, an app to track expenses:

- **Idea**: "We discover the mission: what do we want to create?" Who will use it? What problem does it solve? What should it do?
- **Analysis**: "We explore the terrain and gather tools." Everything it will do, pinned down before the build starts:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| Add an expense | Record its amount, category and date |
| List expenses | Show everything recorded |
| Summary by category | Total the spending in each category |

- **Design**: the structure. How the pieces connect, how someone moves through it, how the software behaves.
- **Development**: build it, from the design. Implement add, list and summarise, then wire them up.
- **Testing**: verify it does what the analysis said. "A checklist, run every time, not once."
- **Deployment**: publish it, "so someone who is not its author can actually use it".
- **Maintenance**: fix bugs, improve what is slow or ugly, keep it running. "Forever."

Three lessons follow. First, **development arrives comparatively late**: three phases happen before anyone types code, so there is a lot of thinking about the code before writing it.

Second, testing is not a one-off event. A check you run once tells you about one moment. The same checklist, run after every change, tells you whether the last change broke something. In this course that checklist is the CI check (ruff, mypy and pytest) that runs on every push.

Third, deployment has a precise test: it is done when someone other than the author can use the program. A program that runs only on your laptop has not been deployed.
key_points: Idea, Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance.
Three phases happen before anyone types code: development arrives late.
Testing is "a checklist, run every time, not once".
Deployed means someone who is not the author can use it.
sections.exam_note_md: A question may describe a decision or an artefact (a feature table, a sketch of the structure, a checklist) and ask for its phase. Analysis pins down what it will do; Design decides how the pieces connect.

sections.heading: Software is living: bugs, features, refactors and tech debt
sections.body_md:
Maintenance is the phase that never ends. "Most software is maintained far longer than it is written." The course treats software as **living and evolving**: the lifecycle is not a finite set of steps that ends in a perfect program which then runs forever unchanged. "The only software that does not change is the one that stays forgotten on a shelf, without ever running."

Slide 19 names four reasons the cycle goes on. Learn the distinctions precisely, because exam stories hinge on them:

| Kind of change | Session 1's words | How to recognise it |
|---|---|---|
| **Bug** | We discover unintended behaviours | The program does something nobody meant it to do; the fix changes behaviour to what was intended |
| **Feature** | We have to add new behaviour | Users can do something they could not do before |
| **Refactor** | The software must connect to new components that replace old ones, or run on a different device | The inside changes; what users get stays the same |
| **Tech debt** | We *willingly* leave something implemented in a way that is not the best possible solution, knowing we will need to improve it | A known, chosen shortcut; nothing is broken yet |

In every case, "we start the cycle again, **back to the Design phase**".

Two contrasts trip people up. A bug is **unintended and discovered**; tech debt is **deliberate and known in advance**. A feature **adds** behaviour; a refactor **keeps** it. Session 7 states the refactor test: "change the structure, keep the behaviour. If the output changes, it was not a refactoring." That is how to read the teacher's sample question 2: renaming variables and splitting a long function "with every test still passing unchanged" is the refactoring, while adding a `--month` option is a feature and fixing a skipped last expense is a bug fix. Its fourth option, replacing the CSV file with a JSON file, is not a refactoring either: every user's existing CSV file stops working, so what users do and see changes. Read slide 19's "new components that replace old ones" as parts inside the program that users never see, such as swapping an unmaintained library for its replacement while the report and the tests stay the same.

The expense-tracker history shows each kind. `Add an add command that writes to data/` (`bc9ef3d`) is a feature. `Replace magic numbers with named constants` (`5e9466d`) and `Rename calculate_totals to total_by_category` (`f3bb801`) are refactors: the report they print is the same as before.
key_points: Most software is maintained far longer than it is written.
Bug: unintended, discovered. Tech debt: deliberate, known.
Feature adds behaviour; refactor changes the structure and keeps the behaviour.
All four send the cycle back to Design.
sections.exam_note_md: The classic shape is four short changes and "which one is the refactoring?" (sample Q2). Ask of each: did the behaviour change, and was the current behaviour intended? Check every option against the output test, including options that only swap a component.

sections.heading: The course on the lifecycle, and the card sort
sections.body_md:
Slide 20 maps the course's five modules onto the phases. They are "ordered by SDLC phase rather than by the problem each removes":

| Phases | Module |
|---|---|
| Idea · Analysis | M1 Starting a project: Agile, Scrum |
| Design · Development | M2 Clean code · M3 Terminal |
| Development · Testing | M2 Testing and TDD |
| Testing · Deployment | M4 Git, review, CI |
| Deployment · Maintenance | M5 Docker, registries, delivery |

Each row pairs two neighbouring phases, and M2 appears in two rows (Design to Testing): practices rarely belong to a single phase. The mid-term covers M1, M2 and M3 (sessions 1–10), so it sits on the phases from Idea to Testing.

The session 1 **card sort** ("The coffee shop") made the same point by hand. Each group had a stakeholder brief, three constraint cards, the seven phases and fourteen decision cards, and dragged every card under "the phase where that decision actually gets made". Then two questions:

1. Which decisions affect **more than one phase**?
2. Which **trade-offs** only become visible once the whole board is laid out?

The coffee-shop deck itself is not available, so here is the idea on the expense tracker. "Total the spending in each category" is decided in Analysis. "Keep reading the file, computing the totals and printing the report in separate functions" is a Design decision. "Store expenses in a CSV file that people can also edit by hand" is made once, in Design, but it reaches almost every later phase: Development (the code that reads it), Testing (the sample files the tests need), Deployment (where the file lives on someone else's machine) and Maintenance (what to do with a broken row). Because so much depends on a decision like that, it is costly to change late.

Trade-offs appear only on the full board. Skipping automated tests makes Development look faster; the cost lands in Testing and Maintenance, columns you were not looking at when you decided. The point of laying out every phase at once is to see where a decision is paid for, not only where it is made.
key_points: M1 Idea·Analysis; M2 Design to Testing; M3 Design·Development; M4 Testing·Deployment; M5 Deployment·Maintenance.
Place a decision where it is actually made, then ask which other phases it touches.
The card sort asks which decisions affect more than one phase; so much depends on them that they are costly to change late.
sections.exam_note_md: A sort question can hand you decisions to place under phases, or ask which decision affects more than one phase. Justify by naming the phases it reaches.

sections.heading: Waterfall: five phases, five documents
sections.body_md:
Session 2 is "project management, not project work": how a team moves from one phase to the next, not how the code gets written. And the answer "changed completely between 1995 and 2005".

The way it used to be done is **Waterfall**: linear, sequential phases, each one finished before the next begins. Software project management in the late 1990s looked like this:

- Requirements fixed early; changing them is costly and discouraged.
- Long cycles: months or years before delivery.
- The customer involved mostly at the start and the end.
- Heavy documentation, up front.

Waterfall has five phases, and each produces a defined output:

| Phase | What happens | Output |
|---|---|---|
| Requirements | Gather everything the system must do | A signed specification |
| Design | Decide the structure before any code | Architecture documents |
| Implementation | Build strictly from the design | Code |
| Testing | Verify against the specification | A test report |
| Deployment & maintenance | Ship it; fix what breaks | A running system |

The key line on slide 5: **"The gate between phases is a document that gets approved."** You leave Requirements when the specification is signed, not when someone has tried a working version. The workshop brief turns this into a rule of the game: once a phase is done it is signed off, and you may not go back and change an earlier phase without a formal change request.

Compare this with session 1's seven phases. Waterfall is not a different set of activities. It is one particular way of moving between them: once, in order, with an approved document at each gate, and with the customer seeing the result near the end.
key_points: Waterfall: linear, sequential; each phase finished before the next begins.
Outputs: signed specification, architecture documents, code, test report, running system.
The gate between phases is an approved document, not working software.
Going back to an earlier phase needs a formal change request.
sections.exam_note_md: Watch for options that give Waterfall an Agile feature, such as a user trying working software between phases. In Waterfall the customer is involved mostly at the start and the end.

sections.heading: Where Waterfall works, and why it fails for software
sections.body_md:
Waterfall assumes the requirements are **known in advance and stable**. When that is true, it works. Slide 6 gives three situations:

- **Bridges, buildings, aircraft, cars.** The requirements really are known up front, changing them mid-build really is ruinously expensive, and regulation demands the documentation.
- **Projects where predictability matters more than speed**: you know early roughly what the finished thing looks like and what it costs.
- **Contracts with a fixed scope and a fixed price.**

Software breaks all three of Waterfall's assumptions:

1. **Requirements change.** The customer sees the first version and understands what they actually wanted. "This is normal, not a failure of analysis."
2. **Feedback arrives too late.** Testing is done near the end, so a wrong assumption made early in the project is only found close to the end.
3. **Integration risk piles up.** Four people build four parts in isolation; they are first combined at the end, and then nothing fits.

Session 2's slide 8 pairs each Waterfall disadvantage with Agile's answer:

| Waterfall disadvantage | Agile's answer |
|---|---|
| Inflexible to change | Iterative: change is expected at any stage |
| Problems found late | Continuous feedback finds them early |
| Testing delayed to the end | Testing integrated into every short cycle |
| Poor fit for evolving requirements | Built for evolving requirements |
| Focus on the plan, not the user | Frequent user involvement drives the product |

Keep both halves in mind. "Waterfall is always wrong" is as weak an exam answer as "Agile is always right". A good way to apply slides 6 and 7 is to ask four questions: how much is known up front, how costly change is, whether a fixed price or a regulator is involved, and how soon you need feedback from real users.

Notice the echoes of session 1, and the difference. "Four people build four parts in isolation" sounds like "four people build four corners", but in Waterfall there *is* a shared plan, the signed specification; the parts still fail to fit because nobody combines them until the end. That is why continuous integration (XP, and this course's CI) matters even when the plan is good. And "feedback arrives too late" is what happens when testing is a phase at the end instead of "a checklist, run every time".
key_points: Waterfall works when requirements are known and stable: bridges, predictability over speed, fixed scope and fixed price, regulation.
Software breaks its assumptions: requirements change, feedback arrives too late, integration risk piles up.
Changing requirements after the first version is normal, not a failure of analysis.
sections.exam_note_md: Scenario questions ask which approach fits a project. Argue from the conditions on session 2's slide 6 and the failures on its slide 7.

sections.heading: Agile and the Manifesto, read correctly
sections.body_md:
**Agile** was formalised in **2001** by practitioners reacting to Waterfall's failures on software. It is **iterative, incremental, adaptable**: build a small working slice, show it, learn, adjust. It delivers working software frequently: weeks, not years. Each cycle goes Plan, Build, Review with user, Learn, and back to Plan.

The phases from session 1 do not disappear. "The same lifecycle phases still happen; they just happen in every cycle, on a small slice, instead of once across the whole project." Incremental means the product grows slice by slice; iterative means you go round the same loop again and improve what is there.

The **Agile Manifesto** states four values. "We have come to value":

| Valued more | over | Valued less |
|---|---|---|
| Individuals and interactions | over | processes and tools |
| Working software | over | comprehensive documentation |
| Customer collaboration | over | contract negotiation |
| Responding to change | over | following a plan |

Then the sentence most people skip: **"While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more."** It is a ranking, not a ban. Agile teams still document, still plan and still sign contracts; when the two sides compete, the left side wins. "Agile means no documentation" and "Agile means no plan" are misreadings, and every Agile cycle starts with Plan.

The twelve principles come in four groups:

| Group | Principles |
|---|---|
| Deliver value continuously | Early and continuous delivery; deliver working software often; working software = progress |
| Expect change; collaborate | Welcome changing requirements; business and developers, daily |
| Trust people; sustainable pace | Motivated individuals, trusted; face-to-face conversation; a pace sustainable indefinitely; self-organising teams |
| Keep improving | Technical excellence; simplicity: maximise work *not* done; reflect and adjust, regularly |

Simplicity is the one people misread. The aim is to maximise the work you do **not** do: no feature nobody asked for, no detail planned for an item that will change before it is built.
key_points: Agile (2001): iterative, incremental, adaptable; working software in weeks, not years.
Plan, build, review with user, learn: the same phases, in every cycle, on a small slice.
"There is value in the items on the right": the values are a ranking, not a ban.
Four principle groups: deliver value continuously; expect change, collaborate; trust people, sustainable pace; keep improving.
sections.exam_note_md: The usual trap is a teammate quoting the Manifesto to drop documentation or planning. Quote the closing sentence and say what the value actually ranks.

sections.heading: Scrum, Kanban, XP, Lean, and what the course borrows
sections.body_md:
Agile is a set of values and principles. Several methodologies turn it into practice, and each prescribes something different:

| Approach | What it actually prescribes | Best when |
|---|---|---|
| Scrum | Fixed-length sprints; roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers); planning, daily, review, retrospective | Feature work with a team of 10 or fewer |
| Kanban | A board of columns; a limit on work in progress; pull the next item when you have capacity | A steady stream of varied requests |
| XP (Extreme Programming) | Engineering practices: pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases | Code quality and change rate are both high |
| Lean | Eliminate waste; optimise the whole flow; decide as late as responsibly possible | Cutting cycle time end to end |

Notice what kind of thing each one prescribes. Scrum organises time and roles. Kanban organises the flow of work on a board. XP prescribes how the code itself is written and integrated: **XP is where TDD comes from**, which you meet in M2. Lean removes waste from the whole process.

**What this course uses** (slide 14):

- Scrum vocabulary for the project: **checkpoints are sprints**, **the Definition of Done is a green CI check**, **the Product Owner is the lecturer**.
- XP's engineering practices as the technical spine: **TDD, CI, small commits**.
- A **Kanban board** to track your group's work.

Session 4 makes the Definition of Done more precise: the green CI check is on every group's list, next to checkable items such as a README.

Slide 15 names what most teams get wrong: "It is not about picking one methodology and following blindly, but borrowing the practices that will help you iterate fast and deliver value." The course is itself the example: words from Scrum, practices from XP, a board from Kanban.

The opposite mistake is to copy the ceremonies and skip the work. A team that holds every Scrum meeting but never tests, pushes one huge commit a week and lives with a red CI check has the vocabulary without the practices. Session 4 makes the same warning: following the Scrum ceremonies is not enough to get real work done.
key_points: Scrum: sprints and roles. Kanban: board, WIP limit, pull. XP: engineering practices. Lean: cut waste, decide late.
XP is where TDD comes from.
The course: Scrum words (checkpoints = sprints, Definition of Done = green CI, PO = lecturer), XP practices (TDD, CI, small commits), a Kanban board.
Borrow practices; do not follow one methodology blindly.
sections.exam_note_md: Expect a situation (a support desk, a feature team, a codebase that changes daily) and a choice of approach. Match it to the "best when" column and say what that approach prescribes.

sections.heading: Plan, then re-plan: the workshop and the real costs of Agile
sections.body_md:
The session 2 workshop took one idea (a bill-splitting app, a student club website, vending machine software, a game) and planned it twice.

**Part 1, as Waterfall.** Five phases, start to finish; for each, two or three bullets on what the group does and what document or artefact it produces. Rule of the game: once a phase is done it is signed off, and going back needs a formal change request.

**Part 2, as Agile.** The same idea, re-planned as short iterations:

1. What is the **smallest version a real person could actually use**? Not a prototype, but something that works, even if it does almost nothing. That is iteration one.
2. The next two or three iterations, each a small usable improvement.
3. Where do you show the work to a user and get feedback?
4. What did switching cost you?

The brief insists on question 4: "Name at least one real downside; Agile is not free." It suggests three: **less up-front certainty about the final scope**, **a fixed price is harder to quote**, and **more coordination overhead**. Then the groups compared: where did the two plans diverge first, and which would you rather be running in month six?

They diverge at the very first step. Waterfall's first output is a signed specification of everything; Agile's first output is a small program a user can try. By month six the Agile team has had several rounds of feedback, while the Waterfall team may not yet have shown anyone working software.

The expense tracker grew this way. Its very first commit, `Add a script that totals expenses by category` (`3e0834f`), already printed a usable report:

```console
$ python tracker.py
Expense report for expenses.csv
----------------------------------------
groceries              6401.78
utilities              3474.15
home                   3442.26
dining                 3345.66
transport              2928.81
health                 1928.13
education              1780.66
entertainment          1395.58
----------------------------------------
TOTAL                 24697.03
```

Filtering by category, the largest expense, packaging and the `add` command arrived in later commits. The backlog brief calls the category total "the first thing it ever did".
key_points: Iteration one is the smallest version a real person could actually use, not a prototype.
Every plan needs a place where a user sees the work and gives feedback.
Agile is not free: less certainty about final scope, harder to quote a fixed price, more coordination.
The two plans diverge at the first output: a signed specification versus a usable slice.
sections.exam_note_md: Open questions ask you to compare the two plans for a given idea and to name one real downside of Agile. A first iteration must be usable software, and a downside must be real.

terms.definition_md: The systematic process of designing, developing, testing and maintaining software using scientific and engineering principles, so that it is reliable, secure, efficient and easy to maintain over time. It goes beyond writing code.
Code that runs for its author and nowhere else, because something it needs exists only on that machine. Session 3 calls it "the single problem this whole course is built to solve".
The seven phases software goes through: Idea, Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Deployment, Maintenance.
The SDLC phase that pins down everything the software will do before the build starts, such as the expense tracker's feature table (add, list, summary by category).
Publishing the software so that someone who is not its author can actually use it.
Fixing bugs, improving what is slow or ugly and keeping the software running, "forever". Most software is maintained far longer than it is written.
Unintended behaviour that is discovered in the software. Fixing it changes the behaviour to what was intended.
New behaviour added on purpose: users can do something they could not do before.
A change to the inside of the software (for example to connect to a new component that replaces an old one) that keeps its behaviour. "If the output changes, it was not a refactoring."
A part willingly left implemented in a way that is not the best possible solution, knowing it will need improving later.

A linear, sequential way to run a project: each phase finished before the next begins, requirements fixed early, long cycles, heavy documentation up front, and an approved document as the gate between phases.
The risk that parts built in isolation do not fit when they are first combined. In Waterfall it piles up until the end.
A way of organising software work, formalised in 2001: iterative, incremental and adaptable, delivering working software in weeks, not years.

Four values that rank individuals and interactions, working software, customer collaboration and responding to change above processes and tools, comprehensive documentation, contract negotiation and following a plan, while still valuing the latter.
An Agile methodology with fixed-length sprints, three roles (Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers) and planning, daily, review and retrospective. Best for feature work with a team of 10 or fewer.
An Agile methodology built on a board of columns, a limit on work in progress, and pulling the next item when there is capacity. Best for a steady stream of varied requests.
An Agile methodology that prescribes engineering practices: pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases. XP is where TDD comes from.
An approach that eliminates waste, optimises the whole flow and decides as late as responsibly possible. Best for cutting cycle time end to end.

The checkable bar every item must meet before it counts as done. The slides map it to "a green CI check", the same for every group; each group writes its own list, which must include that check. CP1's listed three checks: `uv sync && uv run <app> --help` works from a clean clone, the `src/` layout, and a README.
The first Agile iteration in the workshop: something a real person can actually use, even if it does almost nothing. Not a prototype.

traps: **"Agile means no documentation."** The Manifesto ranks working software above comprehensive documentation and adds "while there is value in the items on the right". Agile teams keep the documentation that helps; your CP1 needs a README.
**"Agile means no plan."** Every Agile cycle starts with Plan. "Responding to change over following a plan" means changing the plan when you learn something, not having none.
**"Agile skips phases."** The same lifecycle phases happen in every cycle, on a small slice, instead of once across the whole project.
**"Waterfall is always wrong."** It genuinely works when requirements are known and stable: bridges and aircraft, fixed-scope and fixed-price contracts, regulation that demands documentation.
**"If the requirements changed, the analysis failed."** The customer sees the first version and understands what they actually wanted: "This is normal, not a failure of analysis."
**"Tech debt is another word for bugs."** A bug is unintended and discovered; tech debt is a shortcut taken willingly, knowing it must be improved later.
**"Any change to the code is a refactor."** A refactor changes the structure and keeps the behaviour. A new option is a feature; correcting wrong output is a bug fix.
**"Testing is a phase you do once, at the end."** Session 1: "a checklist, run every time, not once". In this course the CI check runs on every push.
**"It runs on my laptop, so it is deployed."** Deployment means someone who is not its author can actually use it; "works on my machine" is the failure, not the goal.
**"Holding the Scrum meetings makes us Agile."** Slide 15: borrow the practices that help you iterate fast and deliver value. Without tests, CI and small commits, the ceremonies change nothing.

flashcards.back_md: Three phases (Idea, Analysis, Design) happen before anyone types code: there is a lot of thinking about the code before writing it.

flashcards.front_md: "A checklist, run every time, not once": which phase, and why every time?
flashcards.back_md: Testing. A check run once tells you about one moment; repeated after every change, it tells you whether the last change broke something. In the course: CI on every push.

flashcards.front_md: When is software deployed?
flashcards.back_md: When someone who is not its author can actually use it.

flashcards.front_md: Why does maintenance last "forever"?
flashcards.back_md: Software is living: bugs, features, refactors and tech debt keep sending it back to Design. Most software is maintained far longer than it is written.

flashcards.front_md: Bug vs tech debt?
flashcards.back_md: A bug is unintended behaviour that is discovered. Tech debt is a shortcut left in place willingly, knowing it will need improving.

flashcards.front_md: Feature vs refactor?
flashcards.back_md: A feature adds behaviour users can see. A refactor changes the structure and keeps the behaviour: if the output changes, it was not a refactoring.

flashcards.front_md: Where does the cycle start again after a bug, a feature, a refactor or tech debt?
flashcards.back_md: Back at the Design phase.

flashcards.front_md: Slide 20: which module covers Idea and Analysis?
flashcards.back_md: M1 Starting a project: Agile, Scrum.

flashcards.front_md: Card sort, question 1: which decisions does it ask you to find, and why do they matter?
flashcards.back_md: Those that affect more than one phase, such as storing expenses in a hand-editable CSV file (it reaches Development, Testing, Deployment and Maintenance). Because so much depends on them, they are costly to change late.

flashcards.front_md: Waterfall's five phases and their outputs?
flashcards.back_md: Requirements: a signed specification. Design: architecture documents. Implementation: code. Testing: a test report. Deployment and maintenance: a running system.

flashcards.front_md: What is the gate between Waterfall phases?
flashcards.back_md: A document that gets approved. Going back to an earlier phase needs a formal change request.

flashcards.front_md: Where does Waterfall genuinely work?
flashcards.back_md: When requirements are known and stable: bridges, buildings, aircraft, cars; when predictability matters more than speed; fixed-scope, fixed-price contracts; when regulation demands documentation.

flashcards.front_md: Three reasons Waterfall fails for software?
flashcards.back_md: Requirements change (normal, not a failure of analysis); feedback arrives too late; integration risk piles up.

flashcards.front_md: How do you read "working software over comprehensive documentation"?
flashcards.back_md: "While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." A ranking, not a ban.

flashcards.front_md: The four groups of the twelve Agile principles?
flashcards.back_md: Deliver value continuously; expect change, collaborate; trust people, sustainable pace; keep improving.

flashcards.front_md: Scrum vs Kanban: best when?
flashcards.back_md: Scrum: feature work with a team of 10 or fewer, in fixed-length sprints. Kanban: a steady stream of varied requests, pulled from a board with a work-in-progress limit.

flashcards.front_md: Where does TDD come from?
flashcards.back_md: XP (Extreme Programming), along with pair programming, continuous integration and small releases.

flashcards.front_md: What does the course take from Scrum, XP and Kanban?
flashcards.back_md: Scrum vocabulary (checkpoints are sprints, the Definition of Done is a green CI check, the Product Owner is the lecturer), XP's practices (TDD, CI, small commits) and a Kanban board.

flashcards.front_md: What is the first iteration in the Agile re-plan?
flashcards.back_md: The smallest version a real person could actually use: not a prototype, something that works even if it does almost nothing.

flashcards.front_md: Three real costs of switching to Agile, from the workshop brief?
flashcards.back_md: Less up-front certainty about the final scope; a fixed price is harder to quote; more coordination overhead.

flashcards.front_md: The Agile Manifesto's four values: what is valued more, over what?
flashcards.back_md: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. "While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more."

flashcards.front_md: What is Agile's cycle, and what happens to the seven SDLC phases inside it?
flashcards.back_md: Plan, build, review with user, learn, then plan again. The same lifecycle phases still happen in every cycle, on a small slice, instead of once across the whole project.

questions.stem_md: A classmate says: "Software engineering is just a fancier name for programming." Which statement matches the course's definition and shows why the classmate is wrong?

options.text_md: Choosing the best programming language and framework for each new project the team starts
options.why_md: That is one decision inside Design. The definition is about a process that runs across the whole life of the software, not a choice of language.

options.text_md: Writing code quickly enough to meet the client's deadline, with as few bugs as possible
options.why_md: Speed is not in the definition. It is about software that stays reliable and easy to maintain over time, long after the deadline.

options.text_md: A systematic process of designing, developing, testing and maintaining software that stays reliable over time
options.why_md: This is slide 5's definition: programming (developing) is only one part of a structured approach that also covers design, testing and maintenance.

options.text_md: Managing a team's budget, deadlines and meetings so that every software project finishes on time and on budget
options.why_md: That is project management, the subject of session 2. Software engineering includes the technical work of design, testing and maintenance.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 5 defines software engineering as "the systematic process of designing, developing, testing, and maintaining computer software using scientific and engineering principles", and adds that it "goes beyond just writing code". The aim is software that is reliable, secure, efficient and easy to maintain over time. Programming is one activity inside that process (Development). Picking a language and meeting a deadline are decisions within it, and budgets and meetings belong to project management, which session 2 separates from "project work".

questions.stem_md: Session 1 insists that this is "not a Python course". Which statement best describes what the course is about instead?

options.text_md: What happens to your code once teammates get involved and it must run reliably and be easy to change
options.why_md: This is the goal on slide 10, almost word for word: the code you can already write, once three teammates get involved.

options.text_md: Learning Python syntax properly, from loops and functions up to classes, decorators and the standard library
options.why_md: Syntax is assumed: the prerequisites are loops, functions, types and a completed Python course. New constructs arrive "as design tools, not language tourism".

options.text_md: Building web and mobile front ends with graphical interfaces that business users can click through
options.why_md: The project is a terminal program with no web or graphical interface; the brief says removing the interface leaves the parts the course is actually about.

options.text_md: Choosing the best web framework for a business application and learning it in depth
options.why_md: The course teaches no framework: the project is a terminal program, and the tools serve teamwork on code, not the choice of technology.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 10 sets the prerequisites (loops, functions, types, a completed course of basic Python) and states that "syntax is assumed". The goal: "what happens to that little program you wrote once three teammates get involved and it is supposed to run reliably, be easy to change, and trustworthy". The syllabus says the same: the course "is concerned with what happens to code once other people work on it". Every tool that follows (uv, ruff, mypy, pytest, git, Docker) serves that goal, not the learning of more Python.

questions.stem_md: Laia wrote her group's CSV loader in February. In August she opens it to add a currency column and loses an afternoon working out what `d`, `r` and `x` hold, and why one line multiplies by `0.79`. Nothing is broken; she just cannot follow it. Which failure from session 1 is this, with the answer slide 8 gives for it?

options.text_md: No shared plan, four people build four corners; Agile and Scrum
options.why_md: The problem is not what the group agreed to build. Laia cannot read code that already exists.

options.text_md: "Works on my machine", and nowhere else; containerisation and automatic deployment
options.why_md: Nothing suggests the code runs on one machine only. Laia's difficulty is understanding it.

options.text_md: A teammate's code change breaks the build; version control, code reviews and CI
options.why_md: Nobody else changed anything, and the story says nothing is broken.

options.text_md: Six months on, nobody can read it, not even its author; clean code, testing, TDD
options.why_md: Cryptic names and an unexplained number are exactly what makes code unreadable months later, even to the person who wrote it.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6's third failure is "six months on, nobody can read it, not even its author", illustrated on slide 7 by the comment admitting that only god now knows how a routine works. Slide 8 groups it with breaking silently: "unreadable, breaks silently → clean code, testing, TDD". In session 6 terms, `d`, `r` and `x` need real names and `0.79` needs a named constant that says what it is. The other options are real failures, but each needs a different story: a disagreement about what to build, a program that runs only on one laptop, or a shared build that a teammate broke.

questions.stem_md: On Thursday night Pau pushes his change straight to the group's `main` branch. On Friday morning the other three pull, and the project no longer passes its checks for anyone, Pau included. Nobody read his change before it landed and nothing ran automatically when he pushed. Which pair from session 1 fits this story?

options.text_md: Six months on, nobody can read it, not even its author; clean code, testing, TDD
options.why_md: Nobody is struggling to read old code here. The problem is how a change got into the shared project unchecked.

options.text_md: A teammate's code change breaks the build; version control, code reviews, CI
options.why_md: One person's change landed in the shared code with no review and no automatic check, and broke it for everyone.

options.text_md: "Works on my machine", and nowhere else; containerisation, automatic deployment
options.why_md: It fails for everyone, Pau included, so this is not a program that runs on one laptop only.

options.text_md: No shared plan, four people build four corners; Agile and Scrum
options.why_md: The group may agree perfectly on what to build. What failed is the path a change takes into the shared code.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6 lists "a teammate's code change breaks the build" and slide 8 answers it with "version control, code reviews, CI". The story contains the two missing safeguards: nobody reviewed the change, and no automatic check ran on the push. In this course the CI check (ruff, mypy, pytest) runs on every push precisely so that a broken change is visible before the others build on it. Because the project fails for everyone, including the author, "works on my machine" does not fit.

questions.stem_md: Four friends start the Habit tracker project. Nobody writes down what the program should do first. Two weeks later one has built a streak calendar, one a statistics report, one a login system and one an export to Excel. Each part runs, but nobody can record a habit yet. Which failure is this, and what does session 1 put against it?

options.text_md: No shared plan, four people build four corners; Agile and Scrum
options.why_md: Nobody agreed what to build or in what order, so four people built four parts that do not add up to a product.

options.text_md: A teammate's code change breaks the build; version control, code reviews and CI
options.why_md: Nothing is broken: each part runs. The problem is which parts were chosen.

options.text_md: Change one thing, three others break, silently; clean code, testing and TDD
options.why_md: No change is breaking other parts. The parts are simply the wrong ones.

options.text_md: Works on my machine; containerisation and automatic deployment
options.why_md: Nobody reports a part that runs only on its author's laptop.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6's last failure, "no shared plan, four people build four corners", is answered on slide 8 by "Agile, Scrum". Each member made a reasonable part, but without an agreed, ordered plan nobody built the one thing a user needs first: recording a habit. In this course the shared plan is an ordered Product Backlog with the most valuable usable item on top (session 4), and the workshop's first Agile question is "what is the smallest version a real person could actually use?".

questions.stem_md:
Last week Jordi made the report print as a neat table. On his laptop `uv run expenses report` works. Marta clones the repository, `uv sync` finishes without errors, and then:

```console
$ uv run expenses report
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/marta/expense-tracker/.venv/bin/expenses", line 4, in <module>
    from expense_tracker.cli import app
  File "/home/marta/expense-tracker/src/expense_tracker/cli.py", line 6, in <module>
    from tabulate import tabulate
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'tabulate'
```

Jordi replies: "It works on my laptop, so the problem is on your side." What can you conclude?

options.text_md: Jordi is right: the code is fine, so Marta should install `tabulate` by hand on her laptop and carry on
options.why_md: That makes it work on two laptops instead of one. CI and every other teammate still fail, because the project itself does not say it needs `tabulate`.

options.text_md: It is "works on my machine": the code needs a package Jordi has but the project never declares
options.why_md: `uv sync` installed everything the project declares and `tabulate` is still missing, so the dependency exists only on Jordi's machine.

options.text_md: The lockfile is damaged: delete `uv.lock` and `.venv`, then run `uv sync` again to rebuild everything
options.why_md: `uv sync` succeeded, so the lockfile was read correctly. Deleting it changes nothing, because `tabulate` is not in it.

options.text_md: Marta's Python is too new for this project, so she needs to install an older version of Python first
options.why_md: The last line reports a missing module, not a Python version problem; uv already chose the version the project asks for.

questions.explanation_md: Read the last line first: the module `tabulate` is missing on Marta's machine. `uv sync` installs exactly what `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` declare, and it finished cleanly, so the repository Marta cloned never declares `tabulate`. On Jordi's laptop it is installed, either by hand or through a change to `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` that he never committed; either way it runs only there. That is the first failure on slide 6, "works on my machine, and nowhere else", which session 3 calls "the single problem this whole course is built to solve". The fix belongs in the project (declare the dependency, for example with `uv add`, and commit the lockfile) so that everyone, CI included, gets the same versions. Slide 8's longer-term answer is containerisation and automatic deployment.

questions.stem_md:
You remove `frozen=True` from `Expense` so that a typo in an amount can be corrected in place:

```diff
-@dataclass(frozen=True)
+@dataclass
 class Expense:
     date: str
     merchant: str
```

`uv run expenses report` still prints the report and exits with 0. You have not pushed, and nobody else has changed anything. Then you run the tests (output trimmed to the summary):

```console
$ uv run pytest -q
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_expenses_without_duplicates_are_unchanged - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_an_exact_duplicate_is_removed_and_the_first_one_kept - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_same_merchant_on_another_day_is_not_a_duplicate - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_many_copies_of_one_expense_collapse_to_one - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
4 failed, 20 passed in 0.05s
```

In session 1's terms, what did the test suite just do?

options.text_md: It caught a "works on my machine" problem: the tests fail only because of something in your local setup
options.why_md: The failures follow directly from your edit; nothing about the machine changed, and CI would fail in exactly the same way.

options.text_md: It caught a teammate's change breaking the build: someone else broke `remove_duplicates`
options.why_md: Nobody else changed anything and nothing has reached the shared project. The change is yours.

options.text_md: It made "change one thing, others break, silently" visible: your edit broke a function you never touched
options.why_md: One edit in `Expense` broke four tests of a different function, while the program itself still looked fine.

options.text_md: It found a bug in `remove_duplicates`: all four failures are its tests, so fix that function
options.why_md: `remove_duplicates` did not change, and its tests passed before your edit. The failures show where the break surfaces; your change to `Expense` is where it was made.

questions.explanation_md: You changed one line in `Expense`. Four tests in `tests/test_duplicates.py`, a file you never opened, now fail, and the report still runs and exits with 0. Without the tests nothing would have looked wrong until someone called `remove_duplicates`: the textbook case of "change one thing, three others break, silently". Slide 8's answer is "clean code, testing, TDD", and here testing turned a silent break into a red line. The cause is session 8's: `dict.fromkeys` needs hashable items, and `frozen=True` is what made `Expense` hashable. Changing `remove_duplicates` to make the red lines go away would treat the symptom. No teammate or machine is involved, so the other failure modes do not fit.

questions.stem_md:
Before writing any code for the expense tracker, the team writes this table and agrees that it is complete:

| Feature | What it does |
|---|---|
| Add an expense | Record its amount, category and date |
| List expenses | Show everything recorded |
| Summary by category | Total the spending in each category |

In which SDLC phase does this table belong?

options.text_md: Idea, because it says what the app should do and who it is for
options.why_md: Idea asks the broad questions, including "what should it do?". A complete, agreed list of features with what each one does is Analysis (slide 16 shows this very table there), and nothing in it says who the app is for.

options.text_md: Design, because it decides how the app will be built and structured
options.why_md: The table says what each feature does, not how the pieces connect or how a user moves through it; that structure is Design.

options.text_md: Testing, because every row of it can be checked against the finished app
options.why_md: Testing uses this table ("verify it does what the analysis said") but does not produce it.

options.text_md: Analysis, because it pins down all the app will do before the build
options.why_md: Slide 16 shows this very table under Analysis: "everything it will do, pinned down before the build starts".

questions.explanation_md: Slide 16 puts the feature table under Analysis, with the line "Everything it will do, pinned down before the build starts." Idea asks the broad questions (who will use it, what problem does it solve, what should it do); Analysis turns the answers into a complete list of features with what each one does. Design then decides the structure that delivers them, and Testing later checks the program against this table. A useful habit: Analysis is about *what*, Design is about *how the pieces connect*.

questions.stem_md: A group tests their Gradebook by hand the night before CP1: they try ten inputs, all work, and they tick "tested" on their plan. Over the next three weeks they make forty commits and never repeat the check. What is wrong with this, in session 1's terms?

options.text_md: Testing is a checklist run every time, not once; it says nothing about the forty commits since
options.why_md: Session 1's exact point: one run tells you about one moment, and every later change can break what was checked.

options.text_md: Ten inputs are too few; testing is only finished when every possible input has been tried at least once
options.why_md: No checklist covers every input. The flaw is not the size of the check but that it was run once and never again.

options.text_md: Testing belongs after Deployment, so it should wait until the final submission
options.why_md: Testing comes before Deployment in the lifecycle, and Agile integrates it into every short cycle rather than pushing it to the end.

options.text_md: Testing by hand is acceptable only when the person who wrote the code does it
options.why_md: Who runs the check does not fix the problem: a check that is never repeated cannot catch what the next commit breaks.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 17 defines Testing as "verify it does what the analysis said. A checklist, run every time, not once." A one-off check proves only that the program worked on that night. After forty commits, any of which could have broken something, the tick on the plan means nothing. This is why the course automates the checklist: the CI check runs ruff, mypy and pytest on every push, the referee that runs whether or not anyone remembers. The repeated check is also how "change one thing, three others break, silently" stops being silent.

questions.stem_md: One week after topics are settled, group A has 300 lines of code and no agreed list of what the program should do. Group B has a feature table and a sketch of how the pieces connect, and no code yet. A member of group A says group B is "behind". In session 1's terms, which comment is right?

options.text_md: Group A is ahead: Development produces the program, so starting it early saves time
options.why_md: Session 1 says development arrives comparatively late. Code written before anyone agreed what it should do risks being thrown away, or becoming four corners.

options.text_md: Group A is ahead, provided it writes the feature table afterwards to describe its code
options.why_md: Analysis pins down what the app will do before the build starts. A table written afterwards describes the code; it cannot guide it.

options.text_md: Neither is ahead: an Agile team starts by coding and works out the plan as it goes
options.why_md: Every Agile cycle starts with Plan, and the same phases happen in each cycle on a small slice. Agile repeats the phases and keeps their order.

options.text_md: Group B is on track: three phases come before code, and development arrives late
options.why_md: Slide 17: "Development arrives comparatively late. Three phases happen before anyone types code." Group B has outputs from Analysis and Design.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 17: "Development arrives comparatively late. Three phases happen before anyone types code. Notice how there is a lot of thinking about the code prior to writing the code itself." Group B has an Analysis output (the feature table, as on slide 16) and a Design output (how the pieces connect), so its code will be built from something agreed. Group A skipped both, which is how "no shared plan, four people build four corners" begins. Agile does not change this: each short cycle still plans, analyses and designs a small slice before building it.

questions.stem_md: Card sort on the expense tracker: place each decision under the phase where it actually gets made.

items.text_md: Decide that the app is for people who want to see where their money goes each month
items.why_md: Who will use it and what problem it solves: the mission, discovered in Idea.

items.text_md: Agree on the problem it solves: nobody in the flat knows where the shared money goes
items.why_md: What problem does it solve? The mission comes first, before any feature is pinned down.

items.text_md: "Summary by category" totals the spending in each category
items.why_md: A row of the feature table: what the app will do, pinned down before the build.

items.text_md: Adding an expense records its amount, category and date
items.why_md: Another row of the analysis table; it says what a feature does, not how it is built.

items.text_md: Reading the file, computing the totals and printing the report are separate functions
items.why_md: How the pieces connect is the structure, which Design decides.

items.text_md: Sketch how a user moves through the program: which command they type and what the screen shows next
items.why_md: Slide 17: Design covers how someone moves through it and how the software behaves.

items.text_md: Turn the feature table into a checklist to verify the finished program against: each feature does what the table says
items.why_md: Verifying the program against what the analysis said is Testing.

items.text_md: Run the same checklist again after every change, not only before release
items.why_md: "A checklist, run every time, not once."

items.text_md: Publish it so a classmate who is not its author can install and run it
items.why_md: Deployment means someone who is not the author can actually use it.

items.text_md: Write install steps in the README so a stranger can run it without help
items.why_md: Making it usable by someone other than its author is the point of Deployment.

questions.explanation_md: Idea finds the mission (who, what problem). Analysis pins down everything it will do, feature by feature. Design decides the structure: how pieces connect and how a user moves through it. Testing verifies the program against the analysis, every time. Deployment makes it usable by someone who is not its author. When a card seems to fit two columns, ask where the decision is actually *made*; the card-sort follow-up then asks which other phases it affects.

questions.stem_md: A start-up plans its expense app: four months of building, the launch, and then the app's budget drops to zero because "it will be finished". Which idea from session 1 most directly challenges this plan?

options.text_md: Development arrives comparatively late, so four months of building before launch is too long
options.why_md: That point is about the phases before code. It says nothing about what happens after launch, which is where this plan goes wrong.

options.text_md: Deployment means someone who is not its author can use it, so the launch will fail
options.why_md: Nothing suggests the launch fails. The flaw is assuming nothing comes after it.

options.text_md: Maintenance goes on forever: most software is maintained far longer than it is written
options.why_md: The plan ends the lifecycle at launch, but bugs, features, refactors and tech debt keep arriving afterwards.

options.text_md: The methodology lies in how a team moves from one phase to the next
options.why_md: True, but it is about transitions between phases; the plan's flaw is dropping the last phase altogether.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 18: Maintenance is "fix bugs. Improve what is slow or ugly, keep it running. Forever." and "Most software is maintained far longer than it is written." The course treats software as living: "the lifecycle is not a finite set of steps that lead to a perfect program that will run forever without being changed". After launch, bugs are discovered, features are requested, components are replaced and tech debt comes due, and each one sends the cycle back to Design. A budget that stops at launch plans for software that "stays forgotten on a shelf, without ever running".

questions.stem_md: Two days before CP1, the team hard-codes the file name `expenses.csv` instead of letting the user choose a file. They add a backlog item: "Let the user choose the file; the hard-coded name will get in the way when we add a second data file." In session 1's terms, the hard-coded name is:

options.text_md: Tech debt: a known, deliberate shortcut that will need improving later
options.why_md: They chose it willingly and wrote down that it must be improved: slide 19's definition of tech debt.

options.text_md: A bug: the program does something that nobody on the team intended it to do
options.why_md: The program does exactly what the team decided. Nothing unintended has been discovered.

options.text_md: A refactor: the structure changed while the behaviour stayed the same
options.why_md: Nothing was restructured; this is a choice about how to build it now, not a reshaping of existing code.

options.text_md: A feature: it adds new behaviour that users of the program can see and use
options.why_md: Reading one fixed file gives users nothing new; it is a limitation accepted to save time.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 19: "Sometimes we will willingly leave things implemented in a way which is not the best possible solution, knowing that at some point we will need to make an improvement (tech debt)." Both conditions are in the story: the shortcut is deliberate (to hit CP1) and known (the backlog item). That separates it from a bug, which is unintended and discovered later. When the team later allows users to choose the file, that change will add behaviour (a feature) and pay the debt back, and like every such change it starts again at Design.

questions.stem_md: The library your loader uses to read files is no longer maintained, so you switch to its replacement. Users run the same commands on the same files and see exactly the same report, and every test passes unchanged. In session 1's terms, which kind of change is this?

options.text_md: A feature, because the code now depends on a new library it did not use before
options.why_md: A feature is new behaviour for users. Users can do nothing they could not do before.

options.text_md: A bug fix, because the old library might have failed one day and broken the report
options.why_md: No unintended behaviour was discovered: nothing was failing.

options.text_md: Tech debt, because working code was changed even though nobody had asked for it
options.why_md: Tech debt is a shortcut left in place on purpose. This change removes a risk; it does not create a shortcut.

options.text_md: A refactor: an old component is replaced inside, and the behaviour stays the same
options.why_md: Slide 19 names exactly this case, and the unchanged tests show the behaviour stayed the same.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 19 describes refactoring as making sure "the software can connect to new components that replace old components, or run on a different device". Session 7 gives the test: "change the structure, keep the behaviour. If the output changes, it was not a refactoring." Both hold here: a new component inside, the same report outside, and every test passing unchanged, which is also what marks the refactoring in the teacher's sample question 2. Using a new library is invisible to users, so it is not a feature, and nothing unintended was found, so it is not a bug fix.

questions.stem_md: Sort each change into the kind of change session 1 describes. The changes with a commit hash in their explanation are real commits from the expense-tracker history; the others are practice examples.

items.text_md: On a teammate's branch, `report --min 20` leaves out an expense of exactly 20.00, although the help text says it ignores amounts *below* the minimum
items.why_md: Unintended behaviour: the program does not do what it says it does.

items.text_md: The report crashes on an empty file instead of printing a total of 0.00
items.why_md: Nobody meant it to crash; the behaviour is discovered, not chosen.

items.text_md: Users can now ask for one category only, such as `dining`, and leave out small amounts
items.why_md: New behaviour users could not get before (commit `6efdf9d`; the category and the minimum were plain command-line arguments until `2ecad20` made them `--category` and `--min`).

items.text_md: A new `add` command writes an expense to `data/expenses.csv`
items.why_md: Users can do something new: record an expense from the command line (commit `bc9ef3d`).

items.text_md: `calculate_totals` is renamed `total_by_category` and `d`, `e`, `r` get real names; the report prints exactly as before
items.why_md: The structure changed and the behaviour stayed the same (commit `f3bb801`). There were no tests yet, so the evidence is an identical report.

items.text_md: Bare numbers such as `40` and `row[3]` become named constants such as `RULE_WIDTH` and `AMOUNT`; the report prints exactly as before
items.why_md: Session 7's extract-constant move: new names, same output (commit `5e9466d`).

items.text_md: To finish CP1, the team keeps every command in one file, `cli.py`, and adds a backlog item to split it once it passes 300 lines
items.why_md: Not the best structure, chosen on purpose and written down for later: tech debt. Nothing is broken yet.

items.text_md: The team knowingly loads every expense into memory, aware it will be slow for huge files, and notes it for later
items.why_md: Not the best possible solution, chosen on purpose and recorded for later improvement.

questions.explanation_md: Two questions sort any change. Did the behaviour change? If not, it is a refactor. If it did, was the old behaviour intended? Unintended and discovered means a bug; deliberately new means a feature. Tech debt is different in kind: it is the decision to leave something below the best solution, knowing it will need improving. All four send the cycle back to Design.
