questions.stem_md: Your group cannot agree on what the program should do first or how to split the work. According to slide 20, which module of the course covers the phases where this gets settled?

options.text_md: M2 Clean code, which sits on Design and Development
options.why_md: M2 is about how code is written once you know what to build.

options.text_md: M4 Git, review and CI, which sits on Testing and Deployment
options.why_md: M4 protects shared code once it exists; it does not decide what to build first.

options.text_md: M1 Starting a project: Agile and Scrum, which sits on Idea and Analysis
options.why_md: Deciding what to build and in what order is Idea and Analysis work, and M1 covers it.

options.text_md: M5 Docker, registries and delivery, which sits on Deployment and Maintenance
options.why_md: M5 is about running the finished program elsewhere and keeping it delivered.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 20 orders the modules "by SDLC phase rather than by the problem each removes": Idea and Analysis go with M1 Starting a project (Agile, Scrum); Design and Development with M2 Clean code and M3 Terminal; Development and Testing with M2 Testing and TDD; Testing and Deployment with M4 Git, review, CI; Deployment and Maintenance with M5 Docker. Slide 8 gives the same answer from the problem side: "no shared plan → Agile, Scrum".

questions.stem_md: In a card sort for the expense tracker, a group places the card "Store expenses in a CSV file that people can also edit by hand" under Design. Which comment about this card is best?

options.text_md: Move it to Analysis: how the expenses are stored is part of what the app must do
options.why_md: The analysis table lists what the app does (add, list, summarise). How the data is stored is a choice about structure, made in Design.

options.text_md: It is made in Design but reaches Development, Testing, Deployment and Maintenance too
options.why_md: The reading code, the test files, where the file lives and how broken rows are handled all depend on it.

options.text_md: Move it to Development: whoever writes the code that reads the file will settle the format
options.why_md: Development builds from the design. Leaving a choice that every later phase depends on to whoever codes first is how four people build four corners.

options.text_md: Leave it in Design and move on: the later phases follow the chosen format at no extra cost
options.why_md: Design is the right column, but the cost is not zero: the reading code, the test files, where the file lives and how broken rows are handled all depend on it.

questions.explanation_md: The card sort's first follow-up question is "Which decisions affect more than one phase?". Storing data as a hand-editable CSV is decided once, in Design, but Development writes the code that reads it, Testing needs sample files, Deployment has to put the file somewhere on someone else's machine, and Maintenance deals with the broken rows people will type. Moving the card, or treating it as free for the later phases, misses that reach, which is what the exercise was designed to make visible. Decisions with that reach are the ones worth getting right early.

questions.stem_md: The card sort's second question asks: "Which trade-offs only become visible once the whole board is laid out?" A group has placed the card "Skip automated tests to reach CP1 sooner" under Development. Which observation answers that question for this card?

options.text_md: The time saved shows under Development; the cost lands under Testing and Maintenance
options.why_md: This is a trade-off between columns, visible only with the whole board laid out: one phase looks cheaper because another pays.

options.text_md: Move the card to Testing, since a decision about tests is made in the Testing phase
options.why_md: Moving the card does not answer the question, and the decision to skip tests is made while building. The question is where it is paid for.

options.text_md: The trade-off stays inside Development: faster coding now, slower coding later on
options.why_md: The cost leaves Development: it lands in Testing and Maintenance, which is why it appears once the full board is laid out.

options.text_md: The trade-off is between Idea and Analysis, because tests are part of what the app does
options.why_md: Tests check what the analysis said; they are not features, and the cost does not land in those phases.

questions.explanation_md: A trade-off that "only becomes visible once the whole board is laid out" is one whose benefit and cost sit in different columns. Skipping tests makes Development look faster. The bill arrives in Testing (session 1: "a checklist, run every time, not once", which now does not exist) and in Maintenance (every later change can break something silently). Looking at a single column, the decision seems free; looking at the whole board, you see who pays. Relocating the card misses the question, which is about consequences across phases.

questions.stem_md: Which description matches Waterfall as session 2 presents it?

options.text_md: Short cycles in which the customer reviews working software at the end of each one
options.why_md: That is Agile's plan, build, review with user, learn. In Waterfall the customer is involved mostly at the start and the end.

options.text_md: A board of columns from which the team pulls the next item when it has capacity
options.why_md: That is Kanban, one of the methodologies that follow Agile principles.

options.text_md: Phases that overlap freely, with requirements refined as the team learns
options.why_md: Waterfall fixes requirements early and finishes each phase before the next begins.

options.text_md: Linear, sequential phases, each finished before the next begins
options.why_md: Slide 4's definition; the requirements are also fixed early.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 4: "Waterfall: linear, sequential phases. Each one finished before the next begins." Its characteristics: requirements fixed early, and changing them is costly and discouraged; long cycles of months or years before delivery; the customer involved mostly at the start and the end; heavy documentation up front. The other options describe Agile's short review cycles, Kanban's board, and an iterative refinement of requirements, which is exactly what Waterfall avoids.

questions.stem_md: A Waterfall team has finished Design for a parking-lot system. What has to happen before Implementation may start?

options.text_md: The architecture documents are approved: the gate is a signed-off document
options.why_md: Slide 5: "The gate between phases is a document that gets approved." Design's output is the architecture documents.

options.text_md: A user tries a working version of the design and gives feedback on what to change
options.why_md: That is Agile's review with the user. Waterfall has no working software at this point, and the customer is involved mostly at the start and the end.

options.text_md: The CI check goes green on the branch where the design documents are kept
options.why_md: CI checks code, and there is no code yet. A green CI check is this course's Definition of Done, not Waterfall's gate.

options.text_md: The Product Owner reorders the backlog and the team plans the next sprint
options.why_md: Product Owner, backlog and sprint are Scrum vocabulary. Waterfall makes one pass with document gates.

questions.explanation_md: Each Waterfall phase has an output: a signed specification, architecture documents, code, a test report, a running system. "The gate between phases is a document that gets approved." Implementation must then "build strictly from the design", so the design has to be signed off first. The workshop's rule of the game follows from this: once a phase is signed off, going back needs a formal change request. Options that mention users trying software, CI or sprints import practices from Agile and from this course.

questions.stem_md: A Waterfall project builds a loans system for a city library. Put each activity or document under the Waterfall phase where it belongs.

items.text_md: Interview every department to gather everything the system must do
items.why_md: Gathering everything the system must do is Requirements.

items.text_md: A 60-page specification, signed by the library before design starts
items.why_md: A signed specification is Requirements' output, and its approval is the gate into Design.

items.text_md: Approved diagrams of the modules and how they connect, drawn before any code
items.why_md: Design decides the structure before any code; its output is the architecture documents.

items.text_md: Decide the database tables and how the modules share them, for the whole system at once
items.why_md: Deciding the structure of everything up front, before any code, is Waterfall's Design.

items.text_md: Developers write the loans module strictly from the approved architecture
items.why_md: Implementation builds strictly from the design, and its output is code.

items.text_md: Check each requirement in the signed specification against the finished system
items.why_md: Waterfall's Testing verifies against the specification, near the end.

items.text_md: A report listing which requirements passed and which failed
items.why_md: A test report is the Testing phase's output.

items.text_md: The system goes live in every library branch, and a team fixes what breaks
items.why_md: Ship it; fix what breaks. The output is a running system.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 5 gives each phase an output, and "the gate between phases is a document that gets approved". Requirements gathers everything the system must do and ends with a signed specification. Design decides the structure before any code and produces architecture documents. Implementation builds strictly from the design and produces code. Testing verifies against the specification and produces a test report. Deployment and maintenance ships it and fixes what breaks, leaving a running system. Of the five outputs, the running system is the first a user can try, and it comes last.

questions.stem_md: Session 2's slide 8 pairs each Waterfall disadvantage with Agile's answer to it. Which pairing is the one on the slide?

options.text_md: Inflexible to change → a signed specification that fixes the scope early
options.why_md: A signed, fixed specification is Waterfall's own method and the cause of the inflexibility. Agile's answer is iteration: change is expected at any stage.

options.text_md: Testing delayed to the end → testing integrated into every short cycle
options.why_md: This row is on the slide: each short cycle includes its own testing, so nothing waits for the end.

options.text_md: Focus on the plan, not the user → a longer Requirements phase with more interviews
options.why_md: More up-front analysis is still a focus on the plan. Agile's answer is frequent user involvement throughout.

options.text_md: Problems found late → a larger test team brought in for the final months
options.why_md: A bigger test at the end still finds problems at the end. Agile's answer is continuous feedback that finds them early.

questions.explanation_md: The table on slide 8: inflexible to change → iterative, change is expected at any stage; problems found late → continuous feedback finds them early; testing delayed to the end → testing integrated into every short cycle; poor fit for evolving requirements → built for evolving requirements; focus on the plan, not the user → frequent user involvement drives the product. Each wrong option answers a Waterfall weakness with more Waterfall: a firmer specification, a longer Requirements phase, a bigger test at the end. Agile's answers share one move: do the thing earlier and more often, in short cycles, with the user involved.

questions.stem_md: Which of these projects does session 2 suggest Waterfall genuinely fits?

options.text_md: A start-up's first app for an untested market, where the idea changes every few weeks
options.why_md: Requirements are unknown and moving: the case Agile is built for.

options.text_md: An IT help desk handling a steady stream of small, varied requests from all departments
options.why_md: That is Kanban's "best when" on slide 13: a steady stream of varied requests.

options.text_md: A fixed-price, fixed-scope system for a regulator that demands full documentation
options.why_md: Known, stable requirements, a fixed scope and price, and regulation that demands documentation: slide 6's conditions.

options.text_md: A student club website whose committee changes its mind after every single meeting
options.why_md: Evolving requirements are "a poor fit" for Waterfall; Agile is "built for evolving requirements".

questions.explanation_md: Slide 6: "Waterfall assumes the requirements are known in advance and stable. When that is true, it works." It names bridges and buildings (requirements known up front, change ruinously expensive, regulation demands documentation), projects where predictability matters more than speed, and "contracts with a fixed scope and a fixed price". The regulated, fixed-price system ticks every condition. The start-up and the club have moving requirements, and the help desk is a stream of varied requests, Kanban's best case.

questions.stem_md: After nine months, a client sees the first version of their booking system and says: "Now that I see it, what we actually need is something different." The project manager concludes: "Our analysis failed. Next time we spend longer on Requirements." What does session 2 say?

options.text_md: The manager is right: a complete enough specification, written with more care, prevents later changes
options.why_md: Session 2 rejects this: no amount of up-front analysis stops a customer learning what they want from a real version.

options.text_md: Requirements changing after a first version is normal, not a failed analysis; show software sooner
options.why_md: Slide 7's own words, and Agile's answer: frequent user involvement, weeks rather than nine months.

options.text_md: The client is at fault: once the specification is signed, the requirements are fixed for good
options.why_md: The contract may say so, but the slide's point is that this is how software requirements behave. Leaning on the contract is contract negotiation over collaboration.

options.text_md: The problem was integration risk: the parts were built separately and combined too late
options.why_md: Integration risk is about parts built in isolation not fitting. Here the client's understanding of what they need changed.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 7 lists "requirements change" as the first reason Waterfall fails for software: "The customer sees the first version and understands what they actually wanted. This is normal, not a failure of analysis." Spending longer on Requirements treats a normal event as a mistake. The answer on slide 8 is structural: frequent user involvement and short cycles, so the first version a client sees arrives after weeks, when a change is cheap, rather than after nine months.

questions.stem_md: In month 1 of a Waterfall project, the signed specification assumes that every bank export has four columns. The test team starts in month 10 and finds that real exports have five, so importing fails on every real file. Rewriting the import delays the launch by two months. Which explanation fits best?

options.text_md: Requirements change: the customer changed their mind about the file format halfway through
options.why_md: Nobody changed their mind. The assumption was wrong from the very start.

options.text_md: Integration risk piles up: parts built in isolation do not fit when they are combined
options.why_md: The mismatch is between the program and real data, not between parts built by different people.

options.text_md: The gate failed: the specification should never have been signed off in month 1
options.why_md: The specification was signed as the process requires. What went wrong is how late anything tested it.

options.text_md: Feedback arrives too late: an early wrong assumption is only found by testing near the end
options.why_md: A month-1 mistake surfaced in month 10, because Waterfall's testing waits for the end.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 7's second reason: "Feedback arrives too late. Testing is done near the end, so a wrong assumption early in the project is only found close to the end." Every detail fits: the assumption dates from month 1, the first test against real data happens in month 10, and the fix now costs two months. Requirements change would need someone to change their mind; integration risk would need separately built parts that fail to fit. Agile's answer from session 2's slide 8 is "testing integrated into every short cycle": one real bank file in the first iteration would have exposed the fifth column within weeks.

questions.stem_md: A Waterfall team builds a parking-lot system from a signed specification that everyone has read. For six months each of the four developers works alone on one part: tickets, pricing, payments and reports. In month 7 they combine the parts for the first time. Tickets record the stay in hours, pricing expects minutes, and the reports read a file that no other part writes. Which explanation fits best?

options.text_md: Requirements changed: the client saw the system and realised it wanted something else
options.why_md: The client has not seen anything yet and nobody changed the specification. The clash is between the parts themselves.

options.text_md: "Works on my machine": each part runs for its author and nowhere else
options.why_md: Each part may run anywhere. The trouble is that the parts do not fit each other once combined, and no machine fixes that.

options.text_md: Integration risk piled up: parts built in isolation were first combined at the end
options.why_md: Slide 7's third reason: four parts built separately for six months meet in month 7 and do not fit.

options.text_md: No shared plan: four people built four corners because nobody agreed what to build
options.why_md: There is a shared plan, the signed specification, and each developer built the agreed part. What was missing was combining the parts early and often.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 7: "Integration risk piles up. Four people build four parts in isolation; they are first combined at the end, and then nothing fits." It sounds like session 1's "four people build four corners", and that is the trap: there the team has no shared plan, while here the plan exists and is signed. The parts still clash because a specification cannot pin down every detail two parts must agree on (hours or minutes, which file), and nobody checks until month 7. A longer specification would not have saved them; combining the parts every day would. That is why XP's continuous integration, and this course's CI check on every push, matter even when the plan is good.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about Agile matches session 2?

options.text_md: The lifecycle phases still happen, in every short cycle, on a small slice of the product
options.why_md: Slide 10: the same phases "just happen in every cycle, on a small slice, instead of once across the whole project".

options.text_md: Agile drops the Design and Testing phases so that the team can deliver working code faster
options.why_md: Nothing is dropped; slide 8 says testing is integrated into every short cycle.

options.text_md: Agile was formalised in the late 1990s as a stricter, documented form of Waterfall
options.why_md: It was formalised in 2001 by practitioners reacting against Waterfall's failures; the late 1990s is when Waterfall dominated.

options.text_md: Agile replaces the seven lifecycle phases with four new ones: plan, build, review, learn
options.why_md: Plan, build, review with user, learn is the loop each cycle goes round; inside it the same lifecycle phases still happen, on a small slice.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 10 defines Agile: formalised in 2001 by practitioners reacting to Waterfall's failures on software; iterative, incremental, adaptable ("build a small working slice, show it, learn, adjust"); working software delivered frequently, in weeks rather than years. The cycle is Plan, Build, Review with user, Learn. The key sentence is that "the same lifecycle phases still happen". Agile changes how often you go through them and on how much of the product.

questions.stem_md: Your teammate says: "The Agile Manifesto values working software over comprehensive documentation, so we can skip the README." What is the best reply?

options.text_md: Agreed: in Agile, the working code itself is all the documentation a project really needs
options.why_md: This reads "over" as "instead of". The Manifesto never says documentation has no value.

options.text_md: Agreed for now: documentation belongs at the very end, once all the code is finished
options.why_md: That moves documentation to the end, which the Manifesto never says. It ranks values; it does not schedule documents.

options.text_md: No: the right side still has value; working software is only ranked above it
options.why_md: The closing sentence: "while there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more".

options.text_md: No: the Manifesto actually puts documentation first, ahead of working software
options.why_md: This reverses the value. Working software is on the left, the side valued more.

questions.explanation_md: The four values end with: "While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." It is a ranking, not a ban: when writing a 40-page specification competes with shipping working software, working software wins, but useful documentation stays. A README is exactly the documentation that helps: the project brief's bar is that a stranger can install and run the program with no help from you, and CP1's Definition of Done required a README saying what the program does and how to run it.

questions.stem_md: A manager announces: "We are Agile now, so no more planning. We respond to change." Which reading of "responding to change over following a plan" is correct?

options.text_md: Plans are waste in Agile, so the team should decide each morning what to build
options.why_md: Every Agile cycle begins with Plan. Deciding afresh each morning invites "four people build four corners".

options.text_md: The team still plans, but changes the plan when it learns something new
options.why_md: The value ranks adapting above sticking to the plan; it does not remove the plan.

options.text_md: Plans are only allowed when the client insists on a fixed-price contract up front
options.why_md: No such rule exists. Agile teams plan every cycle, whatever the contract.

options.text_md: The plan is written once at the start, and only its dates may move later
options.why_md: That is still following a fixed plan. Agile re-plans the content after each review with the user.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 10's cycle is Plan, Build, Review with user, Learn, and back to Plan: planning happens in every cycle. The fourth value says the team values responding to change more than following a plan, and the closing sentence keeps value in the plan itself. What Agile drops is the single, fixed, up-front plan that must be followed to the end. A team with no plan at all is not more Agile; it is the "no shared plan" failure from session 1.

questions.stem_md: A new team spends its first three weeks comparing project-management tools and configuring boards, labels, automations and rules for how tickets move between columns. The four members have not yet sat down together to talk about the product. Which Manifesto value are they getting backwards?

options.text_md: Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
options.why_md: No customer or contract appears in the story.

options.text_md: Responding to change over following a plan
options.why_md: Nothing has changed yet, and they have not made a product plan to follow.

options.text_md: Working software over comprehensive documentation
options.why_md: They have written no product documentation either. What they over-invest in is tooling and process.

options.text_md: Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
options.why_md: Three weeks on tools and process rules, and no conversation between the people: the right-hand side put first.

questions.explanation_md: The first value reads "individuals and interactions over processes and tools". This team has done the reverse: it has invested everything in tools and in rules for how work moves, before the people have even talked about what to build. The tools may be useful later (there is value on the right), but session 2's point is that the conversation comes first. The other values concern customers and contracts, plans versus change, and documents versus software, none of which is what this team over-values.

questions.stem_md: On the Fortune Cookie project, the basic `fortune` command already works. Nil then spends a week building a plugin system "so that any future kind of fortune can be added without touching the code". Nobody has asked for other kinds of fortune. He says this follows the principle "welcome changing requirements". Which principle is he actually breaking?

options.text_md: Face-to-face conversation
options.why_md: Talking more might have stopped him, but the principle his work contradicts is about the work itself.

options.text_md: Welcome changing requirements
options.why_md: Welcoming change means adapting when a real change arrives. He is building for an imagined one, and this is the principle he cites, not the one he breaks.

options.text_md: Simplicity: maximise work not done
options.why_md: A week on a feature nobody asked for is exactly the work this principle says to avoid.

options.text_md: A pace sustainable indefinitely
options.why_md: One week on one feature is not a pace problem; nobody is overworking.

questions.explanation_md: The "keep improving" group includes "simplicity: maximise work *not* done". Building flexibility for requests that do not exist is work that could have stayed undone; if a new kind of fortune is ever requested, the team can change the code then. The trap is the principle Nil cites: "welcome changing requirements" is about responding to changes that have arrived; Nil is predicting one. The backlog brief makes the same point from another angle: only the top items need detail, because "the rest will change, and detailing them now is wasted work".

questions.stem_md: Each story shows one of the Agile principles at work. Sort it into the principle's group on slide 12.

items.text_md: The team shows a working version to users every two weeks instead of one big release at the end
items.why_md: Early and continuous delivery; deliver working software often.

items.text_md: Progress is reported as "features a user can run", not as "percentage of the design document written"
items.why_md: Working software = progress.

items.text_md: Halfway through, the client asks for a new report, and the team adds it to the plan instead of refusing
items.why_md: Welcome changing requirements.

items.text_md: A person from the business side answers the developers' questions every day, so no decision waits a week
items.why_md: Business and developers, daily.

items.text_md: The team stops planning weekend work before deadlines, because tired people ship bugs
items.why_md: A pace sustainable indefinitely.

items.text_md: The developers, not a manager, decide who takes which task
items.why_md: Self-organising teams; motivated individuals, trusted.

items.text_md: Every few weeks the team discusses what to change in how it works, and changes it
items.why_md: Reflect and adjust, regularly.

items.text_md: The team drops a planned "export to PDF" feature that no user has asked for
items.why_md: Simplicity: maximise the work not done.

questions.explanation_md: The four groups on slide 12: deliver value continuously (early and continuous delivery, working software often, working software as the measure of progress); expect change and collaborate (welcome changing requirements, business and developers daily); trust people and keep a sustainable pace (motivated individuals, face-to-face conversation, a pace sustainable indefinitely, self-organising teams); keep improving (technical excellence, simplicity, reflect and adjust). Match each story to the principle it shows, then to its group.

questions.stem_md: After launch, a two-person team maintains a university's room-booking tool. Requests arrive every day and vary widely: a broken link, a new report, a question about permissions, a calendar bug. Fixed two-week sprints have proved pointless, because priorities change daily. Which approach from slide 13 fits best?

options.text_md: Scrum, because fixed-length sprints keep the team focused on one shared goal
options.why_md: Scrum's "best when" is feature work with a team; daily-changing small requests keep breaking the sprint plan, as the team found.

options.text_md: XP, because pair programming and test-driven development fix bugs faster
options.why_md: XP prescribes engineering practices for writing code; it does not organise a stream of incoming requests.

options.text_md: Waterfall, because each request can be fully specified and signed off first
options.why_md: A signed specification for every small request turns minutes of work into weeks of paperwork.

options.text_md: Kanban, because work is pulled from a board when there is capacity
options.why_md: Slide 13: Kanban (a board, a work-in-progress limit, pull when there is capacity) is best for "a steady stream of varied requests".

questions.explanation_md: Slide 13 lists what each approach prescribes and when it is best. Kanban: "a board of columns; a limit on work-in-progress; pull the next item when you have capacity", best for "a steady stream of varied requests". That is this team: no natural sprint goal, priorities that change daily, and items of very different sizes. Scrum's fixed-length sprints suit feature work by a team of ten or fewer; XP prescribes how code is written; Lean targets cycle time end to end.

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes how this course uses Agile methodologies for the group project?

options.text_md: It follows Scrum by the book, with every ceremony and role, and nothing from other methods
options.why_md: The course deliberately mixes methods; slide 15 warns against following one methodology blindly.

options.text_md: Scrum vocabulary, XP's practices (TDD, CI, small commits) and a Kanban board
options.why_md: Slide 14, item by item: checkpoints are sprints, the Definition of Done is a green CI check, the lecturer is the Product Owner.

options.text_md: Waterfall, with each checkpoint as a gate passed only when an approved document is handed in
options.why_md: Checkpoints are sprints, and the Definition of Done is a green CI check, not an approved document.

options.text_md: Kanban only: no sprints and no Definition of Done, just a shared board of tasks to pull from
options.why_md: The course uses sprints (checkpoints) and a Definition of Done (a green CI check) as well as the board.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 14: "Scrum vocabulary for the project: checkpoints are sprints, Definition of Done is a green CI check, Product Owner is me. XP's engineering practices are the technical spine: TDD, CI, small commits. Kanban board is how you will track your group's work." It is the course practising what slide 15 preaches: borrow the practices that help you iterate fast and deliver value, rather than following one methodology blindly. Note the Waterfall trap: a checkpoint is a git tag that the CI check must pass, not a signed document.

questions.stem_md: Group 7 holds sprint planning, a fifteen-minute daily, a sprint review and a retrospective every sprint, exactly by the book. They have no tests, push one large commit a week, and their CI check has been red for nine days. They describe themselves as "fully Agile". Which judgement fits the course best?

options.text_md: They are Agile: the events are in place, and tests can be added in a later sprint
options.why_md: Every item must meet the Definition of Done when it is finished. With no tests and a red CI check, nothing from the last nine days is done, and "later" keeps moving.

options.text_md: They should switch from Scrum to Kanban, because the meetings are their problem
options.why_md: The meetings are not what is missing. A different board adds no tests and turns no check green.

options.text_md: They copied the ceremonies and skipped the practices: tests, green CI, small commits
options.why_md: XP's practices (TDD, CI, small commits) are the course's technical spine, and they are exactly what this group skipped. Session 4 calls the belief that following the ceremonies is enough an "equally dangerous tendency".

options.text_md: Their work is done: every sprint ended with a review, as the Definition of Done asks
options.why_md: The course's Definition of Done is a green CI check, and theirs has been red for nine days. A review is a Scrum event; it is not the bar an item must meet.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 15: "It is not about picking one methodology and following blindly, but borrowing the practices that will help you iterate fast and deliver value." Slide 14 names those practices for this course: TDD, CI and small commits, with a green CI check as the Definition of Done. By that definition, nothing Group 7 has done in nine days is done. Session 4 adds that following the Scrum ceremonies is not enough to get real work done. Holding the events does not make work done, and changing method, to Kanban for example, leaves the real gap untouched.

questions.stem_md: Your group's Kanban board two weeks before the partial submission: **To do**: 6 cards, **In progress**: 9 cards, **Done**: 1 card. There are four of you. Which change does Kanban, as slide 13 describes it, point to?

options.text_md: Add an "Almost done" column so that the progress becomes visible
options.why_md: Another column relabels the same unfinished work; it finishes nothing.

options.text_md: Move every card back to To do and plan a fresh two-week sprint
options.why_md: That swaps methods. Kanban's own tool for this board is the limit on work in progress.

options.text_md: Set a work-in-progress limit and finish cards before pulling new ones
options.why_md: Nine cards in progress for four people is the problem a WIP limit and pulling only with capacity exist to fix.

options.text_md: Split each in-progress card into smaller cards so that more of them can start
options.why_md: Smaller cards can help, but starting more of them raises the work in progress further.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 13 says Kanban prescribes "a board of columns; a limit on work-in-progress; pull the next item when you have capacity". This board breaks the last two: nine cards in progress for four people means everyone is juggling two or three things, and only one has reached Done. A WIP limit (for example, one or two cards per person) forces the group to finish before starting, so cards actually reach Done. That matters most before a deadline, when a finished, tested feature is worth more than three half-built ones.

questions.stem_md: Which approach on slide 13 prescribes each practice, or is described as best in each situation?

items.text_md: Fixed-length sprints, with planning, daily, review and retrospective
items.why_md: Scrum organises work into time-boxed sprints and their events.

items.text_md: A Product Owner, a Scrum Master and Developers
items.why_md: Scrum's three roles.

items.text_md: Best for feature work with a team of 10 or fewer
items.why_md: Scrum's "best when" on slide 13.

items.text_md: A board of columns with a limit on work in progress; pull the next item when you have capacity
items.why_md: Kanban organises the flow of work on a board and keeps work in progress under a limit.

items.text_md: Best for a steady stream of varied requests
items.why_md: Kanban's "best when": no sprint goal, just the next most important request.

items.text_md: Pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases
items.why_md: XP prescribes engineering practices; it is where TDD comes from.

items.text_md: Best when code quality and change rate are both high
items.why_md: XP's "best when": its practices keep code safe to change often.

items.text_md: Eliminate waste and optimise the whole flow
items.why_md: Lean's focus is waste across the whole process.

items.text_md: Decide as late as responsibly possible
items.why_md: Lean delays decisions until the information to make them exists.

items.text_md: Best for cutting cycle time end to end
items.why_md: Lean's "best when" on slide 13.

questions.explanation_md: Each approach prescribes a different kind of thing. Scrum organises time and roles (sprints; Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers; planning, daily, review and retrospective) and suits feature work by a team of ten or fewer. Kanban organises flow (a board, a WIP limit, pull when there is capacity) and suits a steady stream of varied requests. XP prescribes how code is written and integrated (pair programming, TDD, CI, small releases) for when quality and change rate are both high. Lean removes waste across the whole flow, decides as late as responsibly possible, and targets cycle time end to end.

questions.stem_md: A team of six already works in two-week Scrum sprints on a payments program. It adds features every day and releases often. Each release breaks something that used to work, and nobody dares to change the oldest parts of the code. Which approach from session 2's slide 13 should the team borrow from to target this problem?

options.text_md: Scrum: tighter fixed-length sprints and clearer roles to keep the team focused
options.why_md: They already run Scrum and the breaks continue. Session 4: "Scrum organises the work; it does not do it", with "no engineering practices at all".

options.text_md: XP: test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases, pairing
options.why_md: XP prescribes engineering practices and is best when code quality and change rate are both high, which describes this team.

options.text_md: Kanban: a board with a work-in-progress limit, pulling items as capacity allows
options.why_md: Kanban organises the flow of requests. It says nothing about how the code is written or checked.

options.text_md: Lean: eliminate waste and decide late, so that the end-to-end cycle time falls
options.why_md: Lean speeds up the whole flow. This team's problem is changes that break old behaviour, and a faster flow would spread them sooner.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 13: XP prescribes "engineering practices: pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration, small releases", and is best when "code quality and change-rate are both high". This team changes code daily and keeps breaking old behaviour, session 1's "change one thing, three others break, silently". Tests written first and run on every integration turn those silent breaks into red checks before release. Scrum, Kanban and Lean organise the work or its flow; none of them prescribes how the code is written or checked. Session 4 says it of Scrum directly: "Scrum organises the work; it does not do it." Slide 15's advice fits: borrow the practices that help, whatever the framework.
questions.source_ref: S2 slides 13, 15; S4 slide 14; S1 slides 6, 8

questions.stem_md: In the workshop, a group re-plans a bill-splitting app as Agile. Which first iteration fits the brief's "smallest version a real person could actually use"?

options.text_md: Type in who paid what for one shared dinner and see who owes whom
options.why_md: It works and solves a real sliver of the problem, even though it does almost nothing else.

options.text_md: A clickable mock-up of every screen, to show the client the full vision
options.why_md: A mock-up is a prototype; the brief says "not a prototype but something that works".

options.text_md: The complete database design for every feature planned for the year
options.why_md: A design document is Waterfall's Design output. Nobody can use it.

options.text_md: The first half of every feature, so all of them can be finished together later
options.why_md: Half-features cannot be used. That is a layer across the whole product, not a slice.

questions.explanation_md: The brief's first Agile question is: "What is the smallest version a real person could actually use? (Not a prototype but something that works, even if it does almost nothing.) That is your first iteration." Splitting one dinner works end to end: input, calculation, result. A user can try it and say what is missing, which is the point of the review step in plan, build, review with user, learn. Mock-ups, design documents and half-built features all postpone the first moment a real person uses the software.
questions.source_ref: S2 slide 17; Moodle activity brief (15 Sep)

questions.stem_md: The workshop's last Agile question is "What did switching cost you?". Which answer names a real downside that the brief expects?

options.text_md: Users see working software later than they would have in the Waterfall plan
options.why_md: The reverse is true: Agile puts working software in front of users within weeks.

options.text_md: Testing has to wait until the final iteration, when everything has been built
options.why_md: The reverse again: testing is integrated into every short cycle.

options.text_md: Requirements can no longer change once the first iteration has started
options.why_md: Agile is built for evolving requirements; change is expected at any stage.

options.text_md: A fixed price is harder to quote, since the final scope is not pinned down
options.why_md: One of the three costs the brief lists, alongside less up-front certainty and more coordination.

questions.explanation_md: The brief asks: "What did switching cost you? (Less up-front certainty about final scope? Harder to quote a fixed price? More coordination overhead?) Name at least one real downside; Agile is not free." Because the scope is discovered cycle by cycle, nobody can promise on day one exactly what the finished product contains, which makes a fixed price harder to quote. Each wrong option names a Waterfall weakness and pins it on Agile.

questions.stem_md: Two groups plan the same vending machine program, one as Waterfall and one as Agile. Where do the two plans first diverge?

options.text_md: At Testing: the Agile plan tests every iteration, while Waterfall tests near the end
options.why_md: A real difference, but not the first: long before Waterfall reaches its Testing phase, the plans' very first outputs are different kinds of thing.

options.text_md: At the first output: a signed specification versus a small program a user can try
options.why_md: From day one the plans produce different kinds of thing: Waterfall a document, Agile working software.

options.text_md: Nowhere: the Agile plan is simply the same Waterfall plan cut into two-week pieces
options.why_md: Agile does not slice a fixed plan; each cycle is re-planned after the review with the user.

options.text_md: At Design: the Agile plan skips architecture and starts coding on the first day
options.why_md: Agile keeps the phases: each cycle plans and designs a small slice before building it (slide 10).

questions.explanation_md: The workshop asks "where did the two plans diverge first?". Waterfall's first phase, Requirements, produces "a signed specification" of everything the system must do, and nothing usable exists until the end. Agile's first iteration is "the smallest version a real person could actually use", so the first output is working software in front of a user. The Testing option names a real difference, but not the first one. The option that cuts the Waterfall plan into two-week pieces is the subtle trap: Agile is not a fixed plan chopped into sprints. What a later cycle builds depends on what the team learned from the review of the earlier one.
questions.source_ref: S2 slides 5, 10, 17; Moodle activity brief (15 Sep)

questions.stem_md:
Session 1's analysis table lists three features for the expense tracker: add an expense, list expenses, summary by category. This is how the demo project was actually built:

```console
$ git log --oneline --reverse v0.1
3e0834f Add a script that totals expenses by category
6efdf9d Filter by category and ignore small amounts
c746d38 (tag: v0.0) Print the largest expense
a953d05 Turn the script into a uv package
2ecad20 Move the report into the package behind a typer CLI
bc9ef3d Add an add command that writes to data/
89afbe1 (tag: v0.1) Add a README and the MIT licence
```

What does this history show about how it was built?

options.text_md: A usable slice (the category summary) came first; other behaviour arrived in later commits
options.why_md: The first commit already totals by category; filtering, the largest expense and `add` follow one at a time.

options.text_md: All three analysed features were built together in one commit, as in Waterfall's Implementation phase
options.why_md: Behaviour arrives over several separate commits, and `add` appears only in the sixth.

options.text_md: The features were built in the order of the analysis table: add first, then list, then the summary
options.why_md: The summary came first and `add` sixth; no list command appears in this range.

options.text_md: Nothing anyone could use existed until the project became a package in `a953d05`
options.why_md: The first commit was already a script that printed a full report by category.

questions.explanation_md: Read the messages oldest first. `3e0834f` adds a script that totals expenses by category: run as `python tracker.py`, it prints a complete report, so it is usable on day one. Filtering (`6efdf9d`), the largest expense (`c746d38`), packaging (`a953d05`, `2ecad20`) and the `add` command (`bc9ef3d`) follow, each a small step. The backlog brief describes the category total as "the first thing it ever did" and says the `add` item "became expenses add". The analysis said what the app would do; the history shows it delivered slice by slice.
questions.source_ref: expense-tracker v0.0–v0.1; S1 slide 16; S4 slide 25; backlog brief (22 Sep)

questions.stem_md: A friend who missed session 1 asks you to explain the software development lifecycle using the expense tracker.

parts.prompt_md: Which three phases come before Development, and what does each one decide for the expense tracker?
parts.model_answer_md: Idea: who it is for and what problem it solves (knowing where your money goes). Analysis: everything it will do, pinned down before the build: add an expense, list expenses, a summary by category. Design: the structure, how the pieces connect and how a user moves through it.
rubric: Idea, with who will use it or what problem it solves
Analysis, with the feature table (add an expense, list expenses, summary by category) pinned down before the build
Design, with the structure: how the pieces connect or how a user moves through it
parts.weak_answers_md: Listing the three names without saying what each decides earns one mark at most. A common mix-up puts the feature table in Idea or in Design: slide 16 places it under Analysis, "everything it will do, pinned down before the build starts".

parts.prompt_md: What does "testing is a checklist, run every time, not once" mean, and how does this course do it?
parts.model_answer_md: Testing checks the program does what the analysis said. One run describes one moment; the same checklist after every change shows whether the latest change broke something. Here ruff, mypy and pytest run in CI on every push.
rubric: Testing verifies the program against what the analysis said
The same checks are repeated after every change, not done once at the end
Names the course's mechanism: the CI check (ruff, mypy, pytest) on every push
parts.weak_answers_md: "Test it at the end" is the opposite of the point. "Test it thoroughly once" misses "every time". Naming pytest without saying when it runs misses the idea of repetition, which is what catches a change that silently breaks something else.

parts.prompt_md: Why does the course say Maintenance lasts "forever"?
parts.model_answer_md: Most software is maintained far longer than it is written: bugs, new features, replaced components and tech debt keep sending the cycle back to Design.
rubric: States that software keeps changing after release (bugs, features, refactors, tech debt) and is maintained far longer than it is written
parts.weak_answers_md: "Because there are always bugs" is only part of it: it misses features, refactors and tech debt, and the idea that software is living and only stops changing when nobody runs it.

questions.explanation_md: This is the lesson of slides 15 to 19 in one answer. The strong version uses the expense-tracker example for each phase, keeps Analysis (what it will do) apart from Design (how the pieces connect), explains why repeating the checklist matters, and ties Maintenance to the four reasons the cycle goes on.

questions.stem_md:
Read this account from a group working on the Library manager project:

> "In week 2 each of us picked a part to build without agreeing on an order: Marc did fines, Júlia did search, Arnau did reports and I did a login. On Friday Arnau pushed straight to `main`, and from then on nobody's copy passed the checks. When we finally got it running, Júlia's search only worked on her laptop: it needed a package she had installed by hand."

parts.prompt_md: Name the three failures from session 1 in this story, each with the sentence that shows it.
parts.model_answer_md: No shared plan, four people build four corners: each picked a part with no agreed order. A teammate's change breaks the build: Arnau's push to `main` broke the checks for everyone. Works on my machine, and nowhere else: the search needed a package installed only on Júlia's laptop.
rubric: No shared plan / four people build four corners, tied to the parts picked without an agreed order
A teammate's change breaks the build, tied to Arnau's push to `main`
Works on my machine, tied to the package installed by hand on Júlia's laptop
parts.weak_answers_md: "Bad teamwork" or "bugs" is too vague: use the session 1 names. Calling Arnau's push "works on my machine" confuses two failures: the build broke for everyone, which is the shared-build failure. Each failure must be tied to the sentence that shows it.

parts.prompt_md: For each failure, name the answer slide 8 gives and say in a few words how it would have helped.
parts.model_answer_md: No shared plan: Agile and Scrum, an ordered plan so everyone builds the most useful item first. Broken build: version control with review and CI, so a broken change is caught on push. Works on my machine: containerisation and automatic deployment; so far in the course, declaring every package in `pyproject.toml` and committing `uv.lock`.
rubric: No shared plan → Agile, Scrum (a shared, ordered plan)
Broken build → version control, code reviews, CI (checks run on every push, or someone reads the change before it lands)
Works on my machine → containerisation and automatic deployment, or dependencies declared so uv installs the same versions for everyone
parts.weak_answers_md: Answering "testing" for every failure ignores the slide-8 pairings. "Communicate more" is not a course practice. For the package problem, "install it on everyone's laptop" only spreads the problem: the project itself has to declare what it needs.

questions.explanation_md: This mirrors the exam's "name the problem, name the practice" shape. Full marks need the exact session 1 names, each tied to its evidence, and the slide-8 answer for each with a short reason. The most common slip is mixing up "works on my machine" (one machine only) with "a teammate's change breaks the build" (broken for everyone).

questions.stem_md:
Three changes in a Gym workout logger repository:

- **A.** To finish CP1, the team stores personal bests in a plain text file and adds a backlog note: "Move to a CSV with dates; the text file will make the history report hard."
- **B.** A user reports that the app crashes for a member who has not logged any workout yet, instead of saying "no record".
- **C.** The team replaces the text file with a CSV file, converts the existing logs, and the app now also shows the date of each personal best.

parts.prompt_md: Classify A, and say what makes it that kind of change.
parts.model_answer_md: A is tech debt: a shortcut taken willingly to hit CP1, knowing it will need improving; the backlog note shows they knew.
rubric: Tech debt, justified by the deliberate and known shortcut (the backlog note)
parts.weak_answers_md: Calling A a bug misses that nothing unintended happened: the team chose the text file and recorded the cost in the backlog. Calling it a feature misses what makes A special: a weaker solution chosen on purpose, with the cost written down, which is what tech debt means.

parts.prompt_md: Classify B.
parts.model_answer_md: B is a bug: unintended behaviour that a user discovered; the app should say "no record", not crash.
rubric: Bug, because the behaviour is unintended and was discovered by a user
parts.weak_answers_md: "A feature request" is wrong: saying "no record" is what the program was always meant to do. "Tech debt" is wrong too: nobody chose this behaviour; a user discovered it.

parts.prompt_md: Is C a refactor? Explain using the course's test.
parts.model_answer_md: No. C pays back the debt from A, but the app now shows dates, which is new behaviour, so it counts as a feature. A refactor changes the structure and keeps the behaviour; if the output changes, it was not a refactoring.
rubric: Says C is not a refactor because the output changes: dates are now shown
States the test: refactoring changes structure and keeps behaviour (if the output changes, it was not a refactoring)
Notes that C pays back the tech debt from A
parts.weak_answers_md: "Refactor, because the storage changed" looks only at the inside and ignores that users now see something new. The deciding question is whether the behaviour changed: here it did, because dates now appear on screen.

parts.prompt_md: Where does the cycle start again for all three?
parts.model_answer_md: At the Design phase, as slide 19 says.
rubric: Design
parts.weak_answers_md: "Development" skips deciding how the change fits the existing structure, and "Idea" would restart the whole project. Slide 19 is explicit that bugs, features, refactors and tech debt all go back to Design.

questions.explanation_md: The four kinds of change from slide 19, tested on one story. The marks are for the reasons: deliberate and known (tech debt), unintended and discovered (bug), behaviour changed (a feature, even though it also pays the debt back), and the restart point (Design). Change C is the hard part: a change can repay debt and add behaviour at the same time.

questions.stem_md: A chain of gyms wants a terminal tool for its front desk to log members' workouts and show personal bests. The manager is not yet sure which reports the trainers will want. She asks you to compare Waterfall and Agile for this project.

parts.prompt_md: How would a Waterfall plan run this project, and what moves it from one phase to the next?
parts.model_answer_md: Requirements, Design, Implementation, Testing and Deployment run once, each finished before the next. A phase ends only when its document is approved (signed specification, architecture documents). The manager sees the tool mostly at the start and the end.
rubric: Phases run once, in order, each finished before the next begins
The gate between phases is an approved document (signed specification, architecture documents)
The customer is involved mostly at the start and the end
parts.weak_answers_md: Listing the five phases without saying what moves the project between them misses the key idea: the gate is an approved document, not working software. "Waterfall has no testing" is wrong: it has a Testing phase, near the end.

parts.prompt_md: Why does Agile fit this client better? Say what you would build first.
parts.model_answer_md: She does not know which reports trainers want, so requirements will change once she sees a first version, which is normal. Agile builds a small working slice, shows it, learns and adjusts. First iteration: log a workout and show that member's personal best; trainers try it and say which report comes next.
rubric: Links the choice to this client's uncertain or changing requirements
Describes short cycles with feedback from real users (plan, build, review with user, learn)
Names a first iteration a real person can use (for example, log a workout and see a personal best), not a prototype or a document
parts.weak_answers_md: "Agile is faster" or "Agile is modern" earns nothing: the argument must come from this client's uncertainty. A first iteration such as "design the database" or "a mock-up of all screens" is not usable software.

parts.prompt_md: Name one real downside of choosing Agile here.
parts.model_answer_md: Less certainty up front: we cannot promise the final scope or a fixed price, and the trainers must give time to regular reviews.
rubric: Names a genuine cost from the workshop: less up-front certainty about final scope, a fixed price harder to quote, or more coordination overhead
parts.weak_answers_md: "No downsides" contradicts the brief, which says "Agile is not free". "Users see the software later" or "testing happens at the end" are Waterfall's problems, not Agile's, so they earn nothing here.

questions.explanation_md: The comparison question from the workshop, applied to a new client. A strong answer describes Waterfall fairly (document gates, customer at start and end), argues for Agile from this client's uncertainty rather than from fashion, names a genuinely usable first slice, and admits one real cost.
questions.source_ref: S2 slides 4–8, 10; Moodle activity brief (15 Sep)

questions.stem_md: Your consultancy bids for a fixed-price contract to build an expense-claims system for a public hospital. The scope is written in a tender document, the price is fixed, and an auditor requires full documentation of requirements and tests before the system goes live.

parts.prompt_md: Which approach does session 2 suggest fits this contract, and why? Use the conditions from the slides.
parts.model_answer_md: Waterfall: the requirements are known up front and stable (written in the tender), the contract has a fixed scope and a fixed price, and regulation demands the documentation that Waterfall produces at every gate. Predictability matters more than speed.
rubric: Chooses Waterfall (a plan-driven approach with document gates)
Justifies it with at least two slide-6 conditions: known and stable requirements, fixed scope and fixed price, documentation demanded by regulation, predictability over speed
parts.weak_answers_md: "Agile is always better for software" ignores slide 6. Choosing Waterfall without the conditions earns one mark at most: the marks are for matching this project to where Waterfall genuinely works.

parts.prompt_md: Which reason Waterfall fails for software is still a risk here? Say what would show it.
parts.model_answer_md: Feedback arrives too late: testing happens near the end, so a wrong assumption in the specification (say, about how claims are approved) would only appear in the Testing phase, months later.
rubric: Names one slide-7 risk (requirements change, feedback too late, integration risk) and ties it concretely to this project
parts.weak_answers_md: "Nothing can go wrong because the scope is fixed" misses the point: a fixed scope reduces changing requirements, but testing still comes near the end, so a wrong early assumption is still found late, and parts are still combined late.

parts.prompt_md: Name two practices you would borrow from Agile methodologies even inside this contract, and what each protects against.
parts.model_answer_md: XP's test-driven development, so each part is checked as it is built rather than only in the final Testing phase. Continuous integration with small commits, so parts built by different developers are combined and checked on every push and integration risk does not pile up.
rubric: A concrete practice (TDD, CI, small commits, pair programming) with what it protects against
A second practice with its benefit (for example CI against integration risk, TDD against late feedback)
Links to slide 15: borrow practices instead of following one methodology blindly
parts.weak_answers_md: "Use Scrum" is not a practice to borrow inside a fixed-scope contract, and naming a ceremony (a daily meeting) without saying what it protects against earns little. Slide 15's point is to borrow the practices that help, whatever the overall plan.

questions.explanation_md: A worst-case comparison: the project is one where Waterfall genuinely fits, so the reflex answer "Agile" loses marks. Full marks need the slide-6 conditions, one slide-7 risk that remains, and two engineering practices borrowed from XP with what each protects against.

questions.stem_md:
A new team lead reads the Agile Manifesto and announces three decisions:

- **A.** "No more README or documentation: working software over documentation."
- **B.** "No more planning: we respond to change."
- **C.** "No more contract with the client: collaboration over contracts."

parts.prompt_md: What does the sentence at the end of the four values say, and what does it mean for all three decisions?
parts.model_answer_md: "While there is value in the items on the right, we value the items on the left more." The values are a ranking, not a ban: documentation, plans and contracts keep their value, and the left side wins only when the two compete. So all three decisions misread the Manifesto.
rubric: Quotes or paraphrases the closing sentence: there is value on the right; the left is valued more
Concludes it is a ranking, not a ban, so none of the right-hand items is thrown away
parts.weak_answers_md: Reading "over" as "instead of" is exactly the lead's mistake. Agreeing with any one decision ("documentation is optional in Agile") loses the point that the right side keeps its value.

parts.prompt_md: Choose two of the decisions and say what an Agile team actually does instead.
parts.model_answer_md: Planning: every Agile cycle starts with Plan; the team plans, then changes the plan after reviewing with the user. Documentation: the team keeps what helps, such as a README that tells a stranger how to install and run the program, but skips heavy specifications up front.
rubric: Planning still happens every cycle (plan, build, review with user, learn); what is learned updates the plan
Documentation stays where it adds value (for example a README so a stranger can install and run the program)
The contract still exists, but the team works with the customer rather than negotiating every change against it
parts.weak_answers_md: Restating the value ("responding to change is good") without saying what the team does earns nothing. "Plan less" is vague: say when planning happens (every cycle) and what changes the plan (feedback from the user).

parts.prompt_md: Which failure from session 1 does decision B invite?
parts.model_answer_md: No shared plan, four people build four corners.
rubric: No shared plan / four people build four corners
parts.weak_answers_md: "Change one thing, three others break" is about code that breaks silently, not about the absence of a plan. Without planning, each member decides alone what to build: that is four people building four corners.

questions.explanation_md: Misreadings of the Manifesto are a natural exam question on session 2. The closing sentence answers all three decisions at once; the marks then go to saying concretely what Agile teams still do (plan every cycle, keep useful documentation, keep the contract but collaborate) and to linking "no planning" back to session 1's failure.

questions.stem_md: A client offers your agency a fixed price for the bill-splitting app, and also asks for "a demo every two weeks, after which we will tell you what to change".

parts.prompt_md: Using the workshop's list of costs, explain the tension in what the client is asking for.
parts.model_answer_md: A fixed price assumes a scope known up front, the condition under which Waterfall works. Fortnightly demos with changes are Agile, which gives up certainty about the final scope. The workshop names this cost directly: with Agile a fixed price is harder to quote.
rubric: A fixed price assumes a fixed, known scope (where Waterfall works)
Demos followed by changes mean the scope will move (Agile: less up-front certainty about final scope)
Names the workshop cost: a fixed price is harder to quote
parts.weak_answers_md: "Agile and fixed prices cannot coexist" with no reason earns nothing. The marks are for naming why: a fixed price needs a known scope, and changes every two weeks mean the scope moves.

parts.prompt_md: Suggest a way to keep both, and say what the client gives up.
parts.model_answer_md: Fix the price and the number of two-week iterations, but not the exact feature list. Keep the work ordered by value, so the most useful slice (split one dinner) ships first and each demo decides what comes next. The client gives up a guarantee that every feature imagined today is in the final version.
rubric: Fixes price and time but allows the scope to vary
Orders the work by value so the most useful usable slices come first and each review reorders the rest
States what the client gives up: not every feature imagined today is guaranteed
parts.weak_answers_md: "Charge more" or "refuse the demos" avoids the question. Promising a fixed price, a fixed scope and unlimited changes is the contradiction the question asks you to spot, not a solution.

questions.explanation_md: One step past the workshop. The slides say Waterfall suits fixed-scope, fixed-price contracts and that Agile makes a fixed price harder to quote; a client who wants both forces a choice about which of price, time and scope may move. Fixing time and price and letting the scope flex, with the work ordered by value, is the natural consequence of those two slides. It is reasoning from the slides; the course states no such rule.
questions.source_ref: Moodle activity brief (15 Sep); S2 slides 6, 10

questions.stem_md:
Your teammate removed `frozen=True` from `Expense` so that a typo in an amount can be corrected in place:

```diff
-@dataclass(frozen=True)
+@dataclass
 class Expense:
     date: str
     merchant: str
```

`uv run expenses report` still prints the report and exits with 0. Before anything is pushed, you run the tests (output trimmed to the summary):

```console
$ uv run pytest -q
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_expenses_without_duplicates_are_unchanged - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_an_exact_duplicate_is_removed_and_the_first_one_kept - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_same_merchant_on_another_day_is_not_a_duplicate - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
FAILED tests/test_duplicates.py::test_many_copies_of_one_expense_collapse_to_one - TypeError: unhashable type: 'Expense'
4 failed, 20 passed in 0.05s
```

Your teammate says: "The report works, so these tests are out of date. Delete `tests/test_duplicates.py` and push; CI will be green."

parts.prompt_md: In one sentence, what does this output tell you?
parts.model_answer_md: Four tests of `remove_duplicates` now fail because `Expense` is no longer hashable, while 20 tests still pass: the one-line edit broke a function it never touched.
rubric: States that the four failures are all tests of `remove_duplicates`, a function the edit did not touch, while 20 tests pass, and reads the cause from the message: `Expense` is now unhashable
parts.weak_answers_md: "Four tests failed" only repeats the summary line. Say which function the four tests check, and read the cause from the message, `unhashable type: 'Expense'`, which appeared after the edit. Blaming `remove_duplicates` misses that it did not change: the failures show where the break surfaces, and the edit to `Expense` is where it was made.

parts.prompt_md: Which failure from session 1 did the tests just expose, and which answer from slide 8 caught it?
parts.model_answer_md: "Change one thing, three others break, silently": the report still runs, so nothing looked wrong. Testing, from slide 8's "clean code, testing, TDD", made the break visible before the push.
rubric: Names "change one thing, three others break, silently", tied to the report still working
Names testing (slide 8: clean code, testing, TDD) as what made the break visible before the push
parts.weak_answers_md: "Works on my machine" is wrong: CI would fail in the same way, because the cause is the edit. "A teammate breaks the build" describes what would happen after a push; here the tests caught it first. Naming the failure without saying why it is silent (the report still runs) loses a mark.

parts.prompt_md: Do you accept deleting the tests to get CI green? Give your reasoning.
parts.model_answer_md: No. The tests pin behaviour the program still promises: duplicates dropped, first copy kept. Deleting them hides the break until someone calls `remove_duplicates`, and a green check that runs no tests proves nothing. Fix the cause: restore `frozen=True` and correct a typo by building a corrected `Expense` instead.
rubric: Refuses, because the tests describe behaviour the program still needs (duplicates removed, first copy kept)
Says deleting them hides the break: the crash reaches whoever next calls `remove_duplicates` instead of being caught by CI
Proposes fixing the cause: restore `frozen=True` (revert the edit) and correct typos another way
parts.weak_answers_md: "Yes, the report works" judges the program by one command and ignores the behaviours the tests pin. "No, tests are important" is too vague to score: say what the tests protect and what deleting them would let through. It is the same judgement as refusing `# type: ignore` to get CI green in sample Q9.

questions.explanation_md: This is the teacher's "read tool output" shape (sample Q9) applied to session 1. Read the summary lines first: all four failures are tests of `remove_duplicates`, all with the same `TypeError`, and 20 other tests pass, so a single cause outside that function is the likely story. Session 8 supplies it: `dict.fromkeys` needs hashable items, and `frozen=True` is what made `Expense` hashable. In session 1's terms this is the silent break that testing exists to catch. Deleting the tests would turn CI green by removing the evidence, which is the shortcut the sample paper asks you to refuse.
questions.source_ref: S1 slides 6, 8; S8 (dict.fromkeys, frozen); sample Q9 part 3

questions.stem_md: A group writes a detailed ticket for all forty items of its backlog in week 1, with estimates. By week 5 the client has changed their mind and half of the tickets have to be rewritten. Which approach on slide 13 gives the advice that would have saved that work?

options.text_md: Kanban: limit the work in progress and pull the next item when there is capacity
options.why_md: Kanban limits how many items are open at once. It says nothing about when to write the details of the items that are not open yet.

options.text_md: Lean: eliminate waste and decide as late as responsibly possible
options.why_md: Detailing forty items early, then rewriting half, is waste. Deciding as late as responsibly possible means writing a ticket when the item is about to be built, with the most recent knowledge.

options.text_md: XP: pair programming, test-driven development, continuous integration and small releases
options.why_md: XP governs how code is written and integrated. The problem here is planning detail that goes stale, not engineering practice.

options.text_md: Waterfall: finish the requirements in full before design starts, so that nothing changes later
options.why_md: That is the habit that caused the problem: it assumes the requirements stay put once written. Slide 13 lists Waterfall nowhere among the approaches that follow Agile principles.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 13 lists four approaches that follow Agile principles, and each gives different advice. Lean's is to eliminate waste, optimise the whole flow, and decide as late as responsibly possible. Writing and estimating forty tickets in week 1 is the opposite: detail is created early, when the least is known, and half of it is thrown away. The Product Backlog works the same way (session 4): items near the top are detailed, items near the bottom are left rough, because "estimating item 40 precisely is waste". Kanban and XP are real answers to other problems.

questions.stem_md: The client of a fortune-cookie app is reachable only through a weekly email. The developers have three questions about how a fortune should be formatted. They wait five days for an answer, guess, and half of the guesses turn out to be wrong. Which principle on slide 12 is the group not following?

options.text_md: Technical excellence
options.why_md: The guesses went wrong because nobody answered the questions, not because the code was poorly built.

options.text_md: Business and developers, daily
options.why_md: Slide 12, "expect change; collaborate": the people who decide and the people who build talk every day, so a question waits hours, not a week.

options.text_md: Self-organising teams
options.why_md: The developers can organise their own work. The missing thing is the client's answers.

options.text_md: Simplicity: maximise work not done
options.why_md: The guessed work was done and wasted, but the cause is the missing conversation, not the amount of work.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 12 groups the twelve principles in four. Under "expect change; collaborate" are "welcome changing requirements" and "business and developers, daily". A weekly email makes every question cost five days, and the team fills the gap with guesses; each wrong guess is rework. The principle names the remedy: daily contact between the people who know what is needed and the people who build it. The course's own set-up points the same way: slide 14 says the Product Owner is the lecturer.

questions.stem_md: Your group has working code but no tests, and wants to learn how to write the tests that catch a break before users do. According to slide 20, which module is that, and which phases does it sit on?

options.text_md: M1 Starting a project, on Idea and Analysis
options.why_md: M1 settles what to build and in what order. The tests come after something exists.

options.text_md: M2 Testing and TDD, on Development and Testing
options.why_md: Slide 20 puts testing and TDD with Development and Testing, in the module on clean code and tests.

options.text_md: M3 Terminal, on Design and Development
options.why_md: M3 is about working in the terminal. It does not teach how to write tests.

options.text_md: M5 Docker, on Deployment and Maintenance
options.why_md: M5 is about running the finished program elsewhere. Tests are written well before that.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 20 orders the modules by SDLC phase: Idea and Analysis go with M1 Starting a project; Design and Development with M2 Clean code and M3 Terminal; Development and Testing with M2 Testing and TDD; Testing and Deployment with M4 Git, review and CI; Deployment and Maintenance with M5 Docker. Writing tests is the Development and Testing pair. M4 appears next, because it is where the tests are run on every push, but writing them is M2's job.

questions.stem_md: Two students hand in a program that prints the right dining total today. Ana's is one file with no tests, and works only on her laptop. Bo's is a project with a `pyproject.toml`, a lockfile, tests and a check that runs on every push. Using slide 5's definition of software engineering, what do you say?

options.text_md: Bo's has more of what the definition asks for: software that stays reliable and easy to maintain over time
options.why_md: Slide 5 says the aim goes "beyond just writing code": programs that are reliable and easy to maintain over time. A shared environment, tests and a check on every push are how that is done.

options.text_md: Ana's is better engineered, because a single file is the simplest thing that works
options.why_md: Simple is good, but slide 5's aim is reliability and maintainability over time. One file that works on one laptop is neither.

options.text_md: They are equal, because the program prints the same total
options.why_md: The same output today says nothing about next month, a new teammate or a different laptop. The definition looks past the first run.

options.text_md: Bo's is better only if it has more features than Ana's
options.why_md: Features are not part of the definition. It asks for a systematic process and software that lasts.

questions.explanation_md: Slide 5 defines software engineering as "the systematic process of designing, developing, testing, and maintaining computer software using scientific and engineering principles", and says it "goes beyond just writing code": programs that are reliable, secure, efficient and easy to maintain over time. Both programs print the same total, so the difference is everything around the code. Bo's project can be installed from the lockfile by anyone, has tests that notice a break, and is checked on every push. Ana's can only be judged by running it on her laptop today.
